questions.exp: A lessor accounts for a modification to an operating lease as a new lease from the effective date, treating any prepaid or accrued rent from the original lease as part of the lease payments of the modified lease. Prior income is not restated, and reclassification depends on whether the modified lease meets other criteria.

questions.q: A lessee elects the short-term lease exemption for a class of assets. Which lease qualifies?
choices: A 9-month lease with no purchase option
A 3-year lease with low monthly payments
A 12-month lease with a purchase option the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise
An 18-month lease the lessee may cancel after 12 months with a large penalty
questions.exp: A short-term lease has a term of 12 months or less at commencement and no purchase option the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise, so the 9-month lease qualifies. A reasonably certain purchase option disqualifies a lease even if its term is 12 months, and low payments are not a criterion.

questions.q: Merritt Leasing enters a sales-type lease. The present value of lease payments, including a residual value guaranteed by the lessee, is $80,000, and the present value of the unguaranteed residual is $4,000. What is Merritt's net investment in the lease at commencement?
questions.exp: The net investment equals the lease receivable plus the present value of the unguaranteed residual: $80,000 + $4,000 = $84,000. The $80,000 answer omits the unguaranteed residual, which the lessor keeps as part of its investment.

questions.q: Norris Co. leases a truck and guarantees the lessor that the truck will be worth $10,000 at the end of the lease. Norris expects the truck to be worth $7,000 then. What amount related to the residual value guarantee should Norris include in its lease payments?
questions.exp: A lessee includes only the amount it is probable of owing under a residual value guarantee: $10,000 - $7,000 = $3,000. The lessor, by contrast, includes the full $10,000 guaranteed residual in measuring its lease receivable.

questions.q: Oakley Leasing enters a direct financing lease of equipment with a carrying amount of $180,000 and a fair value of $200,000. The lease receivable plus the unguaranteed residual totals $200,000. What is Oakley's net investment at commencement?
questions.exp: In a direct financing lease, the net investment is the lease receivable plus the unguaranteed residual, reduced by the deferred selling profit: $200,000 - $20,000 = $180,000. The $200,000 answer would recognize the profit at commencement, which only a sales-type lease allows.

questions.q: Preston Leasing's net investment in a sales-type lease is $75,816 at January 1, Year 1. It receives $20,000 at the end of each year for 5 years, and the implicit rate is 10%. What is the net investment at December 31, Year 1?
questions.exp: Interest income is $75,816 x 10% = $7,582, so the year-end balance is $75,816 + $7,582 - $20,000 = $63,398. The $55,816 answer ignores the interest accrued before the year-end payment.

questions.q: Quincy Malls leases retail space under an operating lease for base rent of $60,000 a year plus 2% of the tenant's sales above $1,000,000. The tenant's sales for the year are $1,500,000. What lease income should Quincy recognize for the year?
questions.exp: Variable payments based on sales are recognized as lease income when earned: 2% x ($1,500,000 - $1,000,000) = $10,000, plus the $60,000 base rent, for $70,000. The $90,000 answer applies the 2% to total sales instead of only the sales above the threshold.

questions.q: Ridley Leasing leases equipment with a fair value of $46,000 for 5 years, receiving $10,000 at the start of each year. The rate implicit in the lease is 8% (present value factor for an annuity due of 5 periods at 8% is 4.3121). There is no transfer of ownership, purchase option or specialized asset, and the economic life is 8 years. How should Ridley classify the lease?
questions.exp: The present value of lease payments is $10,000 x 4.3121 = $43,121, or 93.7% of the $46,000 fair value, which is substantially all of fair value, so the lease is sales-type. The 5-year term is not a major part of the 8-year life, but meeting any one criterion is enough.

questions.q: Harbor Arts, an NFP, began the year with $800,000 of net assets with donor restrictions. During the year it received $300,000 of new donor-restricted gifts, earned $40,000 of unappropriated investment return on donor-restricted endowment funds, and satisfied purpose restrictions by spending $250,000 on the restricted programs. What are net assets with donor restrictions at year-end?
questions.exp: Net assets with donor restrictions: $800,000 + $300,000 + $40,000 - $250,000 released = $890,000. Unappropriated return on a donor-restricted endowment stays with donor restrictions, so the $850,000 answer wrongly omits it.

questions.q: An NFP spends donor-restricted cash on the program the donor specified. How is this reported in the statement of activities?
choices: As a reduction of the original contribution revenue in net assets with donor restrictions
As a prior-period adjustment to net assets with donor restrictions
As a reclassification that decreases net assets with donor restrictions and increases net assets without donor restrictions, with the expense reported in net assets without donor restrictions
As an expense reported directly in net assets with donor restrictions
questions.exp: Satisfying a restriction is reported as net assets released from restrictions, a reclassification between the two classes, and all expenses are reported in net assets without donor restrictions (ASC 958-205-45). Expenses are never reported directly in the with-donor-restrictions class.

questions.q: In December of Year 1, a donor made an unconditional promise to give River Clinic $100,000 at the end of each of the next five years with no stated use restriction. The present value of the payments is $379,000 and no allowance is needed. How should River Clinic report the promise in Year 1?
choices: No revenue until each payment is received
questions.exp: Unconditional promises are recognized when made, measured at present value, and amounts due in future periods carry an implied time restriction, so $379,000 is reported with donor restrictions. The $500,000 answer ignores discounting of multi-year pledges.

questions.q: In Year 2, River Clinic records $22,000 of discount accretion on a multi-year unconditional pledge it recognized at present value in Year 1. How should the accretion be reported?
choices: As investment return, net of investment expenses
As interest income in net assets without donor restrictions
As a reduction of fundraising expense
questions.exp: Accretion of the discount on a promise to give is reported as contribution revenue, in the net asset class of the original contribution (ASC 958-310). Treating it as interest income is the common mistake; the pledge is not a lending arrangement.

questions.q: A foundation promises Elm Shelter $1 for every $1 Elm raises from other donors, up to $50,000, and the promise lapses for any unmatched amount after June 30 of next year. By December 31, Elm's year-end, it had raised $30,000 of qualifying gifts. How much contribution revenue from the foundation should Elm recognize this year?
questions.exp: A matching grant is a conditional promise with a barrier and right of release; revenue is recognized as the barrier is overcome, here for the $30,000 matched so far. The $50,000 answer treats the full conditional promise as unconditional.

questions.q: Under ASC 958-605 as amended by ASU 2018-08, a promise to give is conditional when the agreement contains which of the following?
choices: Both a barrier that must be overcome and a right of return of assets or right of release from the obligation
A payment schedule extending beyond one year
A requirement to report to the donor on how funds were spent
Any donor stipulation limiting the use of the assets
questions.exp: A conditional contribution requires both a barrier (such as a measurable performance-related hurdle) and a right of return or release. A limitation on use alone is a donor restriction, not a condition, so the contribution is recognized now with donor restrictions.

questions.q: A state agency awards a university $400,000 to research a public health issue. Results will be published publicly and the agency obtains no proprietary rights or other direct benefit. How should the university classify the award?
choices: Exchange transaction, because the agency selected the research topic
Exchange transaction recognized under ASC 606 as research is performed
Agency transaction recorded as a liability to the state
Contribution, because the general public rather than the agency receives the benefit
questions.exp: Under ASU 2018-08, a transfer is an exchange only if the resource provider receives commensurate value; benefits to the general public do not count as commensurate value to the grantor, so the award is a contribution (often conditional). Choosing the topic does not make the agency a customer.

questions.q: Members of Valley Museum pay $100 annual dues and receive free admission, a magazine and shop discounts with a total fair value of about $100. How should the museum account for the dues?
choices: As contribution revenue with donor restrictions released monthly
As exchange revenue recognized over the membership period
As contribution revenue when the dues are received
As an agency transaction with no revenue recognized
questions.exp: When members receive benefits commensurate with the dues paid, the dues are an exchange transaction recognized as performance obligations are satisfied over the membership year. Only the portion of dues exceeding the value of benefits would be a contribution.

questions.q: During the year, Pine Hospital received these donated services: a licensed electrician rewired a wing ($12,000 value), volunteers staffed the gift shop ($20,000 value), and a CPA prepared the annual information return for free ($6,000 value), a service Pine would otherwise have purchased. How much contributed services revenue should Pine recognize?
questions.exp: Contributed services are recognized only if they create or enhance nonfinancial assets (the rewiring, $12,000) or require specialized skills, are provided by people with those skills and would otherwise be purchased (the CPA, $6,000): $12,000 + $6,000 = $18,000. Gift shop volunteering requires no specialized skill, so the $38,000 answer is wrong.

questions.q: Under ASU 2020-07, how must an NFP present contributed nonfinancial assets such as donated food, equipment and services?
choices: Only in the notes, with no amount recognized in the statement of activities
As a separate line item in the statement of activities, apart from contributions of cash and other financial assets, with disaggregation by category in the notes
Combined with cash contributions in a single contributions line
Netted against the related program expenses on the statement of activities
questions.exp: ASU 2020-07 requires gifts-in-kind to be presented as a separate line item and disaggregated by category, with disclosure of monetization or use policies, donor restrictions and valuation techniques. It did not change recognition, so disclosure-only treatment is wrong.

questions.q: Oak Theater, an NFP, sold 400 tickets to its annual gala at $250 each. The fair value of the dinner and entertainment each attendee received was $90. How much contribution revenue should Oak recognize from ticket sales?
questions.exp: Each ticket is part exchange and part contribution: 400 x ($250 - $90) = $64,000 contribution, and 400 x $90 = $36,000 exchange revenue. The $100,000 answer treats the full price as a gift and ignores the benefit attendees received.

questions.q: A donor transfers $1,000,000 of securities to a charitable remainder annuity trust and names Lake College as trustee and remainder beneficiary. The trust pays the donor $50,000 a year for life; the present value of the expected annuity payments is $420,000. What contribution revenue should Lake College recognize at inception?
questions.exp: As trustee, Lake recognizes the $1,000,000 of trust assets, a $420,000 annuity liability and the $580,000 difference as contribution revenue with donor restrictions, because the remainder is time-restricted until the trust terminates. Reporting it without donor restrictions ignores that time restriction.

questions.q: A donor places $2,000,000 in a perpetual trust administered by an unrelated bank. Willow Shelter has an irrevocable right to receive the trust's income forever but will never receive the trust assets. How should Willow report the arrangement at inception?
choices: Recognize a beneficial interest offset by a liability to the bank
Recognize a beneficial interest and contribution revenue with donor restrictions, measured at fair value
Disclose the arrangement only, since the bank controls the assets
Recognize contribution revenue without donor restrictions only as income is received
questions.exp: A beneficiary with an unconditional right to cash flows from a perpetual trust held by a third party recognizes its beneficial interest at fair value (usually the fair value of the trust assets) as contribution revenue with donor restrictions (perpetual). Recognizing only income as received ignores the unconditional right that already exists.

questions.q: Under a charitable lead trust administered by a bank, Birch Hospital will receive $40,000 a year for ten years, after which the remaining trust assets go to the donor's children. How should Birch recognize the arrangement at inception?
choices: No recognition, because the remainder goes to the donor's heirs
Contribution revenue without donor restrictions of $400,000
Contribution revenue equal to the full fair value of the trust assets
Contribution revenue with donor restrictions measured at the fair value of its beneficial interest, typically the present value of the expected payments
questions.exp: In a lead trust the NFP is entitled only to the lead payments, so it recognizes a beneficial interest equal to their present value as contribution revenue with donor restrictions (time-restricted until received). The undiscounted $400,000 ignores time value, and the full trust value includes the heirs' remainder.

questions.q: A community foundation receives $75,000 from a donor with instructions to transfer it to a specific food bank. The foundation has no variance power. How should the foundation and the food bank report the transfer?
choices: The foundation recognizes contribution revenue and a grant expense; the food bank discloses the gift
Both entities recognize $75,000 of contribution revenue
The foundation recognizes an asset and a liability; the food bank recognizes contribution revenue and a receivable
The foundation recognizes contribution revenue; the food bank recognizes nothing until it receives cash
questions.exp: Without variance power the foundation is an agent or intermediary, so it records the cash and a liability to the food bank, while the specified beneficiary recognizes the contribution and a receivable (ASC 958-605-25). Recognizing revenue at both entities would double count one gift.

questions.q: A donor gives $75,000 to a community foundation, suggests that it go to a particular food bank, and explicitly grants the foundation unilateral power to redirect the gift to another beneficiary. How should the foundation report the receipt?
choices: As contribution revenue of the suggested food bank
As contribution revenue of the foundation
As a liability to the suggested food bank
As an agency transaction disclosed in the notes only
questions.exp: Explicit variance power gives the foundation control over the assets, so the foundation recognizes the contribution and the suggested beneficiary does not. Recording a liability is the treatment when no variance power exists.

questions.q: At June 30, Birch Services reports cash of $300,000 (including $40,000 a donor restricted for a building to be built in three years), receivables of $200,000 (of which $60,000 are due in 18 months) and investments of $900,000 (of which $700,000 is perpetual endowment corpus). No endowment appropriation is expected in the next year. What financial assets are available to meet general expenditures within one year?
questions.exp: Available: cash $300,000 - $40,000 restricted = $260,000; receivables $200,000 - $60,000 = $140,000; investments $900,000 - $700,000 = $200,000; total $600,000. The $640,000 answer forgets the building-restricted cash, which cannot be used for general expenditures.

questions.q: Which liquidity information does ASU 2016-14 require NFPs to provide?
choices: Qualitative information on how the entity manages liquid resources to meet cash needs for general expenditures within one year, and quantitative information on the availability of financial assets
A statement of cash flows prepared using the direct method
Liquidity ratios with comparisons to industry averages
A classified statement of financial position separating current and noncurrent items
questions.exp: ASU 2016-14 requires qualitative disclosure of liquidity management and quantitative disclosure of financial assets available for general expenditures within one year of the balance sheet date. It does not require a classified balance sheet; sequencing by liquidity or other presentation remains acceptable.

questions.q: Under current ASC 958 requirements, which NFPs must present an analysis of expenses by both function and nature?
choices: Only NFPs with public debt outstanding
Only voluntary health and welfare entities
All NFPs, in one location: the face of the statement of activities, a separate statement, or the notes
Only NFPs that elect to present an operating measure
questions.exp: ASU 2016-14 extended the function-and-nature analysis to all NFPs and requires it in one location. Limiting it to voluntary health and welfare entities reflects the superseded rule, which is why that answer tempts candidates.

questions.q: Maple Society mailed a brochure containing educational information about heart health and a request for donations, at a total cost of $80,000. The purpose and content criteria for joint activities are met, but the mailing list was selected solely on the basis of recipients' past giving. How should the $80,000 be reported?
choices: Allocated between program services and fundraising based on relative content
questions.exp: Joint costs can be allocated to program services only if the purpose, audience and content criteria are all met; an audience chosen solely for likelihood of giving fails the audience criterion, so all costs are fundraising (ASC 958-720-45). Allocation is permitted only when all three criteria are met.

questions.q: The fair value of Ash College's donor-restricted endowment fund falls to $900,000, below the $1,000,000 original gift amount the donor required to be maintained. How is the $100,000 deficiency reported?
choices: As a reduction of net assets with donor restrictions
As a liability to the donor
In the notes only, with no effect on net assets
As a reduction of net assets without donor restrictions
questions.exp: Under ASU 2016-14, accumulated losses on underwater donor-restricted endowments reduce net assets with donor restrictions, with disclosure of the fair value, original gift amount and deficiency. Charging the shortfall to net assets without donor restrictions was the superseded practice.

questions.q: The board of Cedar Hospice designates $500,000 of cash from unrestricted gifts as a quasi-endowment to be invested long term. How should these assets be classified?
choices: Net assets with donor restrictions, time-restricted
A separate third class of board-designated net assets
Net assets with donor restrictions, perpetual in nature
Net assets without donor restrictions, with board designations permitted on the face or in the notes
questions.exp: Only donors create restrictions; a board designation is an internal decision the board can reverse, so the assets remain without donor restrictions, and the designation may be presented or disclosed. A separate third class does not exist under ASC 958.

questions.q: In Year 1, Aspen Center received a $1,200,000 gift restricted to constructing a facility. Construction was paid in Year 2, and the facility was placed in service on January 1, Year 3, with a 30-year life. The donor did not specify how long the facility must be used. When are the restricted net assets released?
choices: $1,200,000 in Year 2 as construction costs are paid
$1,200,000 in Year 3 when the facility is placed in service
$40,000 per year over 30 years beginning in Year 3
questions.exp: ASU 2016-14 requires the placed-in-service approach absent explicit donor stipulations, so the full $1,200,000 is released when the facility is placed in service in Year 3. Releasing over the useful life was an option eliminated by that standard.

questions.q: In the statement of cash flows of an NFP, how should cash received from a donor restricted to purchasing long-lived equipment be classified?
questions.exp: Cash contributions restricted for long-term purposes, such as acquiring long-lived assets or establishing an endowment, are financing inflows (ASC 230-10-45-14). Investing is tempting because equipment is involved, but the later purchase is the investing outflow, not the gift.

questions.q: During Year 1, Spruce Alliance received unconditional pledges of $250,000, of which 8% are expected to be uncollectible. It also received a $40,000 pledge contingent on Spruce obtaining a matching federal grant, which it has not yet obtained. What total contribution revenue from pledges should Spruce recognize in Year 1?
questions.exp: Unconditional pledges are recognized net of estimated uncollectibles: $250,000 x 92% = $230,000; the $40,000 pledge is conditional and is not recognized until the barrier is overcome. The $270,000 answer wrongly includes the conditional pledge.

questions.q: How should an NFP report expenses, including those funded by donor-restricted gifts, in its statement of activities?
choices: As decreases in net assets with donor restrictions until the restriction expires
Split between the two classes based on the funding source
As decreases in net assets without donor restrictions
In the net asset class that provided the funding
questions.exp: All expenses are reported as decreases in net assets without donor restrictions; restricted funding is reflected through a release from restrictions. Reporting expenses in the class that funded them is the common error.

questions.q: Fir Society received a $25,000 gift restricted to a summer camp program and spent it on the camp in the same reporting period. Which reporting treatment is permitted?
choices: Report it as without donor restrictions if the entity has a policy to do so, applies it consistently and discloses it
Report it as with donor restrictions with no release until the next period
Report it as an exchange transaction because the program was delivered
Report it as without donor restrictions only if the donor later agrees in writing
questions.exp: ASC 958-605-45 permits reporting restricted contributions whose restrictions are met in the same period as without donor restrictions, provided the policy is consistently applied and disclosed. Otherwise the gift is reported with donor restrictions and released in that same period, not the next.

questions.q: How must an NFP present investment return in its statement of activities under ASU 2016-14?
choices: Net of external and direct internal investment expenses, with no requirement to disclose the netted expenses
Net of all investment expenses, with the netted amount disclosed
Gross, with investment expenses disclosed in the notes
Gross, with investment expenses reported as management and general expenses
questions.exp: ASU 2016-14 requires investment return to be presented net of external and direct internal investment expenses and eliminated the disclosure of those netted expenses. Gross presentation with investment expenses in management and general is no longer appropriate.

questions.q: A museum acquires a painting for public exhibition. The painting will be protected and preserved, and museum policy requires proceeds from sales of collection items to be used to acquire other items or for their direct care. What is the museum's accounting option?
choices: It must capitalize the painting and test it for impairment annually
It must capitalize the painting at cost and depreciate it
It may elect not to capitalize the item as part of a collection
It must expense the painting as program services in all cases
questions.exp: Items meeting the definition of a collection may be left uncapitalized under ASC 958-360, with required disclosures; the ASU 2019-03 direct-care language is included in that definition. Works of art are not depreciated even when capitalized, so the depreciation answer is wrong.

questions.q: Which presentation of net assets is required on an NFP's statement of financial position?
choices: Net assets with donor restrictions and without donor restrictions shown separately, along with total net assets
Separate funds for each restricted gift received during the year
Three classes: unrestricted, temporarily restricted and permanently restricted
A single total net assets amount, with classes disclosed only in the notes
questions.exp: ASU 2016-14 replaced the three classes with two, with donor restrictions and without donor restrictions, which are shown on the face along with total net assets. The three-class model is the superseded presentation.

questions.q: Abbott Corp.'s defined benefit plan had a projected benefit obligation of $1,000,000 at January 1. During the year, service cost was $80,000, the discount rate was 6%, benefits paid were $50,000, and an actuarial loss of $20,000 resulted from a change in assumptions. What is the PBO at December 31?
questions.exp: PBO rollforward: $1,000,000 + $80,000 service + $60,000 interest (6% x $1,000,000) - $50,000 benefits + $20,000 actuarial loss = $1,110,000. The $1,090,000 answer omits the actuarial loss.

questions.q: Benson Co.'s pension plan assets had a fair value of $900,000 at January 1. During the year, the actual return on plan assets was $70,000, the employer contributed $100,000, and the plan paid $50,000 in benefits to retirees. What is the fair value of plan assets at December 31?
questions.exp: Plan assets: $900,000 + $70,000 actual return + $100,000 contributions - $50,000 benefits paid = $1,020,000. The $1,070,000 answer forgets that benefits are paid out of plan assets.

questions.q: For the current year, Carlisle Inc.'s pension plan had service cost of $80,000, interest cost of $60,000, expected return on plan assets of $63,000, actual return of $70,000, amortization of prior service cost of $10,000, and amortization of net actuarial loss of $5,000. What is Carlisle's net periodic pension cost?
questions.exp: Net periodic pension cost uses the expected return: $80,000 + $60,000 - $63,000 + $10,000 + $5,000 = $92,000 (ASC 715-30-35-4). Using the $70,000 actual return gives $85,000; the $7,000 difference is an asset gain deferred in OCI.

questions.q: At January 1, Dexter Co. had a net actuarial loss in AOCI of $180,000, a projected benefit obligation of $1,200,000, and a market-related value of plan assets of $1,000,000. The average remaining service period of active employees is 12 years. What is the minimum amortization of the net loss included in pension cost for the year?
questions.exp: The corridor is 10% of the greater of beginning PBO or market-related value: 10% x $1,200,000 = $120,000; the $60,000 excess is amortized over 12 years = $5,000. The $6,667 answer bases the corridor on plan assets, which are the smaller amount.

questions.q: At December 31, Ellery Corp.'s pension plan had a projected benefit obligation of $1,110,000, an accumulated benefit obligation of $950,000, and plan assets at fair value of $1,020,000. What should Ellery report on its balance sheet for the plan?
questions.exp: ASC 715 requires the funded status—PBO minus fair value of plan assets—on the balance sheet: $1,110,000 - $1,020,000 = $90,000 liability. The $70,000 asset uses the ABO, which is not the measure for defined benefit pension funded status.

questions.q: Fowler Inc.'s pension plan assets had a market-related value of $800,000 at the beginning of the year and an expected long-term rate of return of 8%. The actual return on plan assets for the year was $50,000. What asset gain or loss is recognized in other comprehensive income for the year?
questions.exp: Expected return is 8% x $800,000 = $64,000; actual return of $50,000 is $14,000 below expected, an asset loss deferred in OCI. Calling it a gain reverses the comparison of actual to expected.

questions.q: On January 1, Garner Co. amended its pension plan, granting $240,000 of prior service cost to its 20 active employees. Using the years-of-service amortization method, Garner computed total future service-years of 160. What prior service cost amortization should Garner recognize in the first year?
questions.exp: Under the years-of-service method, the first-year fraction is service-years rendered (20) over total service-years (160): $240,000 x 20/160 = $30,000. The $20,000 answer assumes a 12-year straight-line period not given in the facts.

questions.q: Hartley Corp.'s PBO was $2,000,000 on January 1, immediately before a plan amendment that day increased the PBO by $200,000. The discount rate is 5%. Benefits are paid at year-end. What interest cost should Hartley include in pension cost for the year?
questions.exp: Interest cost is the discount rate times the PBO outstanding during the year, including the amendment effective January 1: 5% x $2,200,000 = $110,000. The $100,000 answer ignores the increase in PBO from the amendment.

questions.q: During the year, Irving Co. purchased annuity contracts that settled 30% of its projected benefit obligation, exceeding the threshold for settlement accounting. Immediately before the settlement, AOCI included a $200,000 net actuarial loss. What settlement loss should Irving recognize in earnings?
questions.exp: In a settlement, the pro rata portion of the unrecognized net loss is recognized in earnings: 30% x $200,000 = $60,000 (ASC 715-30-35-79). Recognizing the full $200,000 ignores that only part of the obligation was settled.

questions.q: Jensen Inc. closed a plant, causing a curtailment that eliminated 25% of the expected future years of service of plan participants. Unamortized prior service cost in AOCI was $80,000 before the curtailment. What curtailment loss arises from the prior service cost?
questions.exp: The prior service cost associated with the eliminated years of service is recognized as a curtailment loss: 25% x $80,000 = $20,000 (ASC 715-30-35-92). Recognizing all $80,000 ignores the remaining 75% of service still expected.

questions.q: Kerr Co.'s net periodic pension cost of $92,000 consists of service cost of $80,000 and other net components of $12,000. None of the cost is capitalized. Under current GAAP, how much pension cost should Kerr include in income from operations?
questions.exp: ASU 2017-07 requires service cost to be reported with other employee compensation in operating income, while the other components ($12,000) are presented outside income from operations. Reporting the entire $92,000 in operations follows the superseded presentation.

questions.q: Lorne Manufacturing's net periodic pension cost was $92,000, including service cost of $80,000. Forty percent of the service relates to production employees. What is the maximum amount of pension cost that may be capitalized in inventory?
questions.exp: After ASU 2017-07, only the service cost component is eligible for capitalization: 40% x $80,000 = $32,000. The $36,800 answer applies 40% to total pension cost, including components that cannot be capitalized.

questions.q: During the year, Mercer Corp.'s pension plan had an actuarial loss on the PBO of $20,000, an asset gain of $7,000 (actual return exceeded expected), amortization of prior service cost of $10,000, and amortization of net loss of $5,000. What is the net effect on other comprehensive income, before tax?
questions.exp: OCI = -$20,000 actuarial loss + $7,000 asset gain + $10,000 + $5,000 reclassified to pension cost = $2,000 net gain. The $13,000 loss counts only the new gains and losses and omits the reclassification adjustments for amortization.

questions.q: Nash Co.'s pension plan was underfunded by $100,000 at January 1. During the year, net periodic pension cost was $92,000, the employer contributed $100,000, and pension-related other comprehensive income was a $2,000 net gain. What is the funded status liability at December 31?
questions.exp: The liability increases with pension cost, decreases with contributions, and decreases with OCI gains: $100,000 + $92,000 - $100,000 - $2,000 = $90,000. The $94,000 answer adds the OCI gain instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: Owens Inc. sponsors a defined contribution plan requiring an employer contribution of 5% of covered salaries. Covered salaries for the year were $2,000,000, and Owens had contributed $80,000 by year-end. What should Owens report for the year?
questions.exp: Defined contribution cost equals the required contribution for the period: 5% x $2,000,000 = $100,000, with the unpaid $20,000 accrued as a liability. Expensing only the $80,000 paid is a cash-basis error.

questions.q: Porter Co. participates in a multiemployer pension plan. Its required contribution for the year was $45,000, of which $40,000 was paid by year-end. Porter's share of the plan's total underfunding is estimated at $2,000,000, and Porter has no plans to withdraw. What should Porter recognize?
choices: $45,000 expense and a liability for its share of the plan's underfunding
questions.exp: A multiemployer plan participant recognizes the required contribution as cost and accrues unpaid contributions; it does not record its share of plan underfunding unless withdrawal is probable (ASC 715-80). Recording the underfunding confuses multiemployer with single-employer accounting.

questions.q: Quill Corp.'s postretirement health plan makes employees fully eligible for benefits at age 55 if they have at least 10 years of service. An employee was hired at age 30 (credited service begins at hire) and is expected to retire at age 62. Over what attribution period should Quill accrue the expected postretirement benefit obligation for this employee?
questions.exp: OPEB cost is attributed from the date of hire (or beginning of credited service) to the full eligibility date: age 30 to 55 = 25 years (ASC 715-60-35-66). Attributing to the expected retirement age of 62 (32 years) is the common trap.

questions.q: Rowan Inc. has an employee whose expected postretirement benefit obligation is $90,000. The employee's attribution period is 25 years, and 10 years have been completed. Ignoring interest, what is the accumulated postretirement benefit obligation for this employee?
questions.exp: The APBO is the portion of the EPBO attributed to service rendered to date: $90,000 x 10/25 = $36,000. The $54,000 answer is the unattributed remainder, and $3,600 is a single year's service cost.

questions.q: At January 1, Sloane Co. had a net actuarial gain of $300,000 in AOCI, a PBO of $2,000,000, and a market-related value of plan assets of $2,500,000. The average remaining service period is 10 years. What is the effect of gain amortization on net periodic pension cost for the year?
questions.exp: The corridor is 10% of the greater amount, here plan assets: $250,000; the $50,000 excess gain amortized over 10 years is $5,000, which reduces pension cost. Using the PBO for the corridor gives $10,000, and amortizing a gain never increases cost.

questions.q: Tilden Corp.'s PBO of $5,000,000 has a duration of 12 years. At year-end, the discount rate increased by 0.5 percentage point. Using duration to approximate the effect, what actuarial gain or loss results from the discount rate change?
questions.exp: Change in PBO is approximately -duration x change in rate x PBO: -12 x 0.5% x $5,000,000 = -$300,000, a decrease in the obligation and thus an actuarial gain. A higher discount rate lowers the present value of benefits, so calling it a loss reverses the direction.

questions.q: Upton Co. had $50,000 of unamortized prior service cost in AOCI. During the year, it amended its plan to reduce benefits, decreasing the PBO by $80,000. How is the amendment reflected?
choices: A $130,000 prior service credit is recorded in AOCI
An $80,000 prior service credit is recorded, while the $50,000 cost continues to be amortized separately
An $80,000 gain is recognized in earnings immediately
The $80,000 credit first reduces the existing prior service cost in AOCI, leaving a $30,000 net prior service credit
questions.exp: A plan amendment that reduces benefits creates a prior service credit in OCI that is first used to reduce any remaining prior service cost in AOCI (ASC 715-30-35-17): $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000 net credit. Recognizing an immediate gain in earnings is not permitted.

questions.q: During the year, Vail Inc.'s pension plan paid $120,000 of benefits to retirees from plan assets. What is the effect of these payments on the plan's funded status reported by Vail?
choices: Increases the net pension liability by $120,000
Decreases the net pension liability by $120,000
Reduces net periodic pension cost by $120,000
questions.exp: Benefit payments reduce both the PBO and plan assets by $120,000, so the difference (funded status) is unchanged and pension cost is unaffected. Only employer contributions change funded status in the direction of the payment.

questions.q: Walden Co.'s plan assets were $1,000,000 at January 1, with an expected rate of return of 8%. On July 1, Walden contributed $200,000 and the plan paid $100,000 of benefits. What expected return on plan assets should Walden use in pension cost, weighting the cash flows for time?
questions.exp: Expected return = 8% x $1,000,000 + 8% x $200,000 x 6/12 - 8% x $100,000 x 6/12 = $80,000 + $8,000 - $4,000 = $84,000. The $88,000 answer weights the contribution but ignores the benefits paid mid-year.

questions.q: Yardley Corp. recognized a $100,000 pre-tax pension loss in other comprehensive income. Its tax rate is 25%. What amount should Yardley report in OCI for the pension loss, net of tax?
questions.exp: OCI items are reported net of tax (or with the tax shown separately): $100,000 x (1 - 25%) = $75,000 loss, with an offsetting deferred tax asset. The $25,000 figure is only the tax effect.

questions.q: Zeller Co.'s PBO was $1,000,000 at January 1. Service cost was $80,000, the discount rate was 6%, and benefits paid at year-end were $50,000. The actuary's year-end valuation reported a PBO of $1,150,000. What actuarial gain or loss arose on the PBO during the year?
questions.exp: Expected PBO is $1,000,000 + $80,000 + $60,000 - $50,000 = $1,090,000; the actual $1,150,000 is $60,000 higher, an actuarial loss. The $150,000 answer treats the entire change in PBO as an actuarial loss, ignoring service cost, interest, and benefits.

questions.q: Ainsley Corp.'s pension plan had service cost of $150,000, a beginning PBO of $3,000,000 with a 5% discount rate, beginning market-related value of assets of $2,600,000 with a 7% expected return, prior service cost amortization of $24,000, and amortization of a net actuarial gain of $8,000. What is net periodic pension cost?
questions.exp: Cost = $150,000 service + $150,000 interest (5% x $3,000,000) - $182,000 expected return (7% x $2,600,000) + $24,000 PSC - $8,000 gain amortization = $134,000. The $150,000 answer adds the gain amortization rather than subtracting it.

questions.q: Bristow Inc. offered special termination benefits of $20,000 per employee to employees who accept within a 30-day window. Fifty employees accepted during the window, and the amount can be reasonably estimated. How should Bristow account for the benefits?
choices: Disclose the offer in the notes only
Recognize $1,000,000 over the employees' remaining service period
Recognize $1,000,000 when the employees accept the offer
Recognize $1,000,000 when the offer is made
questions.exp: Special termination benefits offered for a short period are recognized as a liability and loss when employees accept and the amount can be reasonably estimated (ASC 715-30-25-10): 50 x $20,000 = $1,000,000. Recognition at the offer date is too early because acceptance is required.

questions.q: Crane Co. sponsors an unfunded supplemental executive retirement plan with a PBO of $500,000. Benefits expected to be paid in the next 12 months total $40,000, and the plan has no assets. How should Crane classify the liability on its classified balance sheet?
questions.exp: The current portion of an underfunded plan is the amount by which benefits payable in the next 12 months exceed plan assets: $40,000 - $0 = $40,000 current, with $460,000 noncurrent (ASC 715-20-45-3). Reporting the entire amount as noncurrent ignores the near-term payments from an unfunded plan.

questions.q: Dalton Corp. sponsors two defined benefit plans. Plan One is overfunded by $100,000 and Plan Two is underfunded by $250,000. How should Dalton present the plans on its balance sheet?
choices: A net $150,000 liability, with the overfunded plan disclosed in the notes
questions.exp: ASC 715-20-45 requires all overfunded plans to be aggregated and presented as an asset and all underfunded plans aggregated as a liability; overfunded and underfunded plans may not be netted. The net $150,000 liability answer improperly offsets the two plans.

questions.q: At January 1, Easton Co. had a net actuarial loss in AOCI of $90,000, a PBO of $800,000, and a market-related value of plan assets of $700,000. During the year, Easton incurred an additional $60,000 actuarial loss. The average remaining service period is 15 years. What net loss amortization is included in pension cost for the year?
questions.exp: Amortization is based on the beginning-of-year net loss: corridor = 10% x $800,000 = $80,000; excess = $90,000 - $80,000 = $10,000 / 15 = $667. The $4,667 answer includes the current-year loss, which affects amortization only starting next year.

questions.q: Fenton Inc.'s unfunded postretirement health plan had an APBO of $400,000 at January 1, a discount rate of 5%, service cost of $15,000, and amortization of prior service cost of $5,000. What is Fenton's net periodic postretirement benefit cost?
questions.exp: OPEB cost = $15,000 service + $20,000 interest (5% x $400,000) + $5,000 PSC amortization = $40,000; there is no expected return because the plan is unfunded. Omitting the PSC amortization gives $35,000.

questions.q: During the year, Gilbert Co.'s pension plan paid $120,000 in lump-sum distributions. Service cost was $80,000 and interest cost was $60,000. Gilbert's policy is to apply settlement accounting only when required. Must Gilbert recognize a settlement gain or loss?
choices: No, because total settlements of $120,000 do not exceed service cost plus interest cost of $140,000
Yes, because the payments exceed interest cost
Yes, because the payments exceed service cost
Yes, because any lump-sum payment is a settlement requiring recognition
questions.exp: Settlement accounting may be omitted when the cost of all settlements in the year does not exceed the sum of service cost and interest cost (ASC 715-30-35-82): $120,000 is less than $140,000. Comparing payments to only one component of cost misapplies the threshold.

questions.q: Hale Corp.'s pension formula provides an annual benefit of 2% x years of service x final salary. An employee has 10 years of service, a current salary of $60,000, and a projected final salary of $100,000. What annual benefit is used in measuring the PBO for this employee's service to date?
questions.exp: The PBO uses service to date and projected future salary: 2% x 10 x $100,000 = $20,000. The $12,000 answer uses current salary, which is the ABO measure.

questions.q: Hale Corp. measured an employee's annual pension benefit attributed to service to date at $20,000, payable at the end of each year for 15 years beginning one year after retirement. Retirement is 20 years away, and the discount rate is 5%. What is the PBO for this employee (rounded)?
questions.exp: PV at retirement = $20,000 x 10.3797 (15-year ordinary annuity at 5%) = $207,594; discounted 20 years at 5% (factor 0.37689) = $78,240. The $207,594 answer stops at the retirement date and omits the second discounting step.

questions.q: Irons Co. recognized $10,000 of prior service cost amortization as part of net periodic pension cost, reclassifying it out of AOCI. What is the effect of this amortization on comprehensive income for the year?
questions.exp: The amortization increases pension cost (reducing net income by $10,000) and is an equal reclassification adjustment that increases OCI by $10,000, so total comprehensive income is unchanged. The cost was already in comprehensive income when the prior service cost arose.

questions.q: At December 31, Jarvis Inc.'s pension plan had a PBO of $1,100,000 and plan assets at fair value of $950,000. Jarvis had also accrued a $50,000 contribution for the year that it paid to the plan on January 15. What net pension liability should Jarvis report at December 31?
questions.exp: Plan assets exclude contributions accrued by the employer but not yet paid to the plan, so funded status is $1,100,000 - $950,000 = $150,000. The $100,000 answer improperly treats the unpaid contribution as a plan asset.

questions.q: Keller Corp. has elected to recognize actuarial gains and losses immediately in net periodic pension cost (a mark-to-market policy). This year, it had an actuarial loss on the PBO of $75,000 and an asset gain of $15,000 (actual return exceeded expected). What is the effect of these items on pension cost for the year?
questions.exp: ASC 715 permits any systematic method that recognizes gains and losses at least as fast as the corridor approach, including immediate recognition: $75,000 loss - $15,000 gain = $60,000 increase in pension cost. The $0 answer applies the default deferral in OCI, which Keller did not elect.

questions.q: Linwood Co. began the year with a $150,000 net actuarial loss in AOCI. During the year, it had a $40,000 actuarial loss on the PBO, a $10,000 asset gain, and amortized $6,000 of net loss into pension cost. What is the net actuarial loss in AOCI at year-end?
questions.exp: Ending net loss = $150,000 + $40,000 loss - $10,000 asset gain - $6,000 amortization = $174,000. The $194,000 answer treats the asset gain as an addition to the loss.

questions.q: Arden Builders signs a $1,000,000 fixed-price contract that adds a $200,000 bonus if the project is finished by June 30. Arden estimates an 85% chance of earning the bonus and concludes it is probable that including it will not cause a significant revenue reversal. Using the method that best predicts the consideration, what transaction price should Arden use?
questions.exp: The bonus has only two possible outcomes, so the most likely amount method gives the better prediction: $1,000,000 + $200,000 = $1,200,000. The $1,170,000 answer applies the expected value method ($200,000 x 85%), which suits contracts with many possible outcomes rather than a single binary outcome.

questions.q: Bexley Supply sells 1,000 units at $50 each, with a right of return. Each unit cost $30, and based on experience Bexley expects 5% of units to be returned. What revenue should Bexley recognize on the sale?
questions.exp: Expected returns are variable consideration, so revenue is recognized only for the 950 units not expected to be returned: 950 x $50 = $47,500, with a $2,500 refund liability and a $1,500 asset for the right to recover products (50 x $30). The $50,000 answer ignores the expected returns entirely.

questions.q: When estimating variable consideration, which factor increases the likelihood that including it in the transaction price could result in a significant revenue reversal?
choices: The amount is highly susceptible to factors outside the entity's influence
The entity has extensive experience with similar contracts
The uncertainty is expected to be resolved within a short period
The contract has only a small number of possible consideration amounts
questions.exp: ASC 606-10-32-12 lists susceptibility to factors outside the entity's influence, such as market volatility or third-party judgment, as an indicator that a reversal is more likely. Extensive experience, quick resolution and a small number of outcomes all point the other way and support including the estimate.

questions.q: On January 1, Cordell Labs transfers a functional license to its patented formula to a licensee in exchange for a royalty of 5% of the licensee's sales. At inception Cordell estimated it would earn $150,000 of royalties in Year 1. The licensee's actual Year 1 sales were $2,000,000. How much royalty revenue should Cordell recognize in Year 1?
questions.exp: Under the sales-based royalty exception, royalties on a license of IP are recognized at the later of when the subsequent sale occurs or the performance obligation is satisfied: $2,000,000 x 5% = $100,000. Cordell does not estimate the royalty as variable consideration, so the $150,000 inception estimate is irrelevant.

questions.q: Which license is most likely a symbolic license that provides a right to access intellectual property, with revenue recognized over time?
choices: A license to a franchise brand the franchisor keeps supporting
A license to a drug formula with no further licensor activities
A license to a finished film the licensor will not alter
A license to completed software that works without updates
questions.exp: A brand or trade name has little standalone functionality, and its utility depends on the licensor's ongoing activities that support or maintain it, so it is a symbolic license recognized over the license term. Software, completed films and drug formulas have significant standalone functionality and are generally functional licenses recognized at a point in time.

questions.q: Dalton Brands grants a retailer a 3-year license to use its trademark for a $600,000 upfront fixed fee plus a royalty of 4% of the retailer's sales. The license is symbolic. In Year 1 the retailer's sales total $1,000,000. What total revenue should Dalton recognize in Year 1?
questions.exp: A symbolic license is a right to access, so the fixed fee is recognized over the term ($600,000 / 3 = $200,000) and the sales-based royalty is recognized as sales occur ($1,000,000 x 4% = $40,000), for $240,000. The $640,000 answer treats the fee as earned at a point in time, which applies only to a functional license.

questions.q: Ellery Software has a 2-year term license with a customer that expires December 31, Year 2. In November of Year 2 the customer signs a renewal for Years 3 and 4 and pays the renewal fee. When may Ellery recognize revenue for the renewal?
choices: Ratably from November through the end of Year 4
No earlier than the start of the renewal period on January 1
When the renewal fee is received in cash
When the renewal agreement is signed in November
questions.exp: Revenue for a license renewal cannot be recognized before the beginning of the period in which the customer can use and benefit from the renewed license (ASC 606-10-55-58C). Signing the agreement or collecting cash early does not transfer control of the renewed right.

questions.q: Fairview Systems sells equipment, installation and a 2-year service plan in one contract for $90,000. Standalone selling prices are $60,000 for the equipment, $15,000 for installation and $25,000 for the service plan. How much of the transaction price is allocated to the service plan?
questions.exp: The transaction price is allocated on relative standalone selling prices: $90,000 x ($25,000 / $100,000) = $22,500. The $15,000 answer uses the residual approach, which is allowed only when a standalone selling price is highly variable or uncertain.

questions.q: Granger Co. sells three products, Alpha, Beta and Gamma, with standalone selling prices of $40, $55 and $45. It bundles all three for $100. Granger regularly sells Alpha alone for $40 and Beta and Gamma together for $60. How much of the $100 should be allocated to Beta?
questions.exp: Observable evidence shows the entire $40 discount relates to Beta and Gamma, so Alpha gets $40 and the $60 is split between Beta and Gamma by their standalone prices: $60 x 55/100 = $33.00. The $39.29 answer spreads the discount across all three products ($100 x 55/140), which is wrong when the discount can be traced to specific items.

questions.q: Under ASC 606, when may an entity use the residual approach to estimate a standalone selling price?
choices: Only when the residual amount is equal to or greater than zero
Whenever the contract contains three or more performance obligations
Whenever the entity prefers it to the adjusted market assessment
When the standalone selling price is highly variable or uncertain
questions.exp: The residual approach is permitted only when the standalone selling price of a good or service is highly variable or uncertain, for example because it has not yet been priced or is sold to different customers at very different amounts. It is not a free policy choice, and the number of performance obligations does not matter.

questions.q: Harlow Travel runs a website where customers book hotel rooms. Harlow never controls the rooms, has no inventory risk and the hotels set the prices. A customer pays $400 for a room, and Harlow remits $340 to the hotel. How much revenue should Harlow recognize on the booking?
questions.exp: Harlow does not control the room before it transfers to the customer, so it is an agent and recognizes revenue net, equal to its commission: $400 - $340 = $60. The $400 answer is gross reporting, which applies only to a principal.

questions.q: Inman Tours commits in advance to buy 100 nonrefundable airline tickets at $300 each, sets its own resale prices and bears the loss on unsold tickets. It sells 80 tickets at $380 each, and the other 20 expire unused. What revenue should Inman recognize?
questions.exp: Inman controls the tickets before transfer, bears inventory risk and sets prices, so it is a principal and reports revenue gross: 80 x $380 = $30,400. The $6,400 answer is the net margin on the tickets sold (80 x $80), which an agent would report.

questions.q: Under ASC 606, which of the following is NOT one of the listed indicators that an entity is a principal rather than an agent?
choices: The entity has inventory risk before or after transfer to the customer
The entity bears the customer's credit risk for the amount receivable
The entity has discretion in establishing the price
The entity is primarily responsible for fulfilling the promise
questions.exp: ASC 606-10-55-39 lists primary responsibility for fulfillment, inventory risk and pricing discretion as indicators of control. Credit risk was an indicator under the old guidance but was removed from ASC 606 because it does not show control of the good or service.

questions.q: Jessup Inc. contracts to sell 100 units to a customer at $80 each. After 60 units are delivered, the contract is modified to add 40 more distinct units at $75 each, which is their standalone selling price at that date. What revenue per unit should Jessup recognize for the 40 additional units?
questions.exp: The added units are distinct and priced at their standalone selling price, so the modification is a separate contract and the additional units earn $75.00 each, while the original 40 remaining units still earn $80. The $77.50 answer blends the remaining and added units, which is the treatment when the price does not reflect standalone selling price.

questions.q: Kellner Co. contracts to sell 100 distinct units at $80 each. After 60 units are delivered, the customer agrees to buy 40 more units at $60 each, a price that does not reflect their $75 standalone selling price. What revenue per unit should Kellner recognize for each of the 80 units still to be delivered?
questions.exp: Because the remaining goods are distinct but the added units are not priced at standalone selling price, the modification is treated as terminating the old contract and creating a new one: (40 x $80 + 40 x $60) / 80 = $70.00 per unit. The $74.29 answer is a cumulative catch-up across all 140 units, which applies only when the remaining goods are not distinct.

questions.q: Lowell Construction has a $10,000,000 contract with estimated costs of $8,000,000, a single performance obligation measured by cost-to-cost. At the end of Year 1 it had incurred $4,000,000 of cost and recognized $5,000,000 of revenue. Early in Year 2, a modification raises the price by $2,000,000 and estimated total costs by $1,500,000; the added work is not distinct. What revenue adjustment does Lowell record at the modification date?
questions.exp: A modification that adds work that is not distinct from a partly satisfied performance obligation is accounted for by cumulative catch-up: progress is $4,000,000 / $9,500,000 = 42.105%, so cumulative revenue is $12,000,000 x 42.105% = $5,052,632, an increase of $52,632. The $1,000,000 answer wrongly keeps the old 50% progress measure.

questions.q: Marlow Corp. wins a 3-year service contract. It pays its salesperson a $30,000 commission for winning it, pays outside counsel $5,000 to draft the contract (owed whether or not the deal closed), and spends $2,000 on travel to pitch the client. Marlow expects to recover all costs. What amount should Marlow capitalize as a cost to obtain the contract?
questions.exp: Only incremental costs that would not have been incurred without obtaining the contract are capitalized, so only the $30,000 commission qualifies. Legal and travel costs that are incurred whether or not the contract is obtained are expensed as incurred, which is why the $35,000 and $37,000 answers are wrong.

questions.q: On July 1, Year 1, Nolan Tech pays a $24,000 commission to obtain a 4-year service contract with no expected renewals. Service is provided evenly over the term. What commission expense should Nolan recognize for the calendar year ended December 31, Year 1?
questions.exp: The capitalized commission is amortized on a systematic basis consistent with the transfer of services: $24,000 / 4 years x 6/12 = $3,000. The $24,000 answer applies the practical expedient, which is available only when the amortization period is one year or less.

questions.q: Orton Services pays a sales commission on a new 2-year contract but pays no commission on renewals. It expects the customer to renew twice for 2 years each. Over what period should the capitalized commission be amortized?
choices: The initial term plus the anticipated renewals
Immediately, because the initial term is short
The average customer life of all customers
questions.exp: The asset is amortized over the period the related goods or services are transferred, which includes specifically anticipated renewals when no commensurate commission is paid on renewal. Limiting amortization to the 2-year initial term would understate the period of benefit.

questions.q: When may an entity expense the incremental costs of obtaining a contract as incurred, rather than capitalizing them, under the ASC 606 practical expedient?
choices: When the costs are less than 5% of the contract price
When the amortization period of the asset would be one year or less
When the costs are paid in cash before the contract is signed
When the entity is a private company that elects simplified reporting
questions.exp: ASC 340-40-25-4 allows incremental costs of obtaining a contract to be expensed when the amortization period would be one year or less. There is no materiality percentage or private-company-only test in the expedient.

questions.q: Which of the following costs should be expensed as incurred rather than capitalized as a cost to fulfill a contract with a customer?
choices: General and administrative costs not chargeable to the customer
Allocated supervision costs that relate directly to the contract
Direct labor for setting up a customer's technology platform
Materials used directly in performing the contract
questions.exp: ASC 340-40-25-8 requires general and administrative costs to be expensed unless they are explicitly chargeable to the customer under the contract. Direct labor, direct materials and directly related supervision costs can be capitalized if they generate resources used to satisfy future performance obligations and are expected to be recovered.

questions.q: Paxton Equipment delivers a machine on January 1, Year 1. The customer will pay $1,000,000 on December 31, Year 2. The cash selling price would be the amount that discounts at the customer's 10% borrowing rate. How much revenue should Paxton recognize on January 1, Year 1?
questions.exp: Payment more than a year after delivery indicates a significant financing component, so revenue is measured at present value: $1,000,000 / 1.10^2 = $826,446, with the rest reported as interest income over two years. The $909,091 answer discounts for only one year.

questions.q: Quinlan Retail sells a $100 product and gives the buyer a coupon for 40% off any purchase of up to $50 in the next 30 days. Quinlan is offering 10% off to all customers in the same period, and it expects 80% of coupons to be redeemed. How much of the $100 should be allocated to the coupon?
questions.exp: Only the incremental 30% discount is a material right, so its standalone selling price is 30% x $50 x 80% = $12, and the allocation is $100 x 12/112 = $10.71. The $13.79 answer ignores the 10% discount available to everyone and values the option at $16.

questions.q: Ramsey Manufacturing ships goods to a dealer on consignment. The dealer may return unsold goods and pays Ramsey only after selling them to end customers. When should Ramsey recognize revenue?
choices: When the goods are shipped to the dealer
When the dealer sells the goods to end customers
When the dealer receives and inspects the goods
Ratably over the expected consignment period
questions.exp: In a consignment arrangement, control does not pass to the dealer on delivery because the dealer is not obligated to pay and can return the goods. Ramsey recognizes revenue when control passes, which is when the dealer sells the goods to end customers.

questions.q: Sutton Co. has a contract with two performance obligations, allocated 60% and 40% of the transaction price at inception. After the first obligation is fully satisfied, the transaction price rises by $20,000 because of a change in estimated variable consideration. The change does not relate specifically to either obligation. How much revenue should Sutton recognize immediately?
questions.exp: Changes in the transaction price are allocated on the same basis as at contract inception, and the amount allocated to a satisfied obligation is recognized immediately: $20,000 x 60% = $12,000. Sutton does not reallocate based on updated standalone prices, and the remaining $8,000 is recognized as the second obligation is satisfied.

questions.q: Thayer Consulting has a contract with $400,000 of fixed fees and a performance bonus. Based on a large portfolio of similar contracts, the bonus outcomes are $0 (20% probability), $50,000 (50%) and $100,000 (30%). Thayer concludes the constraint does not limit the estimate. What transaction price should it use?
questions.exp: With many similar contracts and several possible outcomes, the expected value method is most predictive: $0 + $25,000 + $30,000 = $55,000, so the transaction price is $455,000. The $450,000 answer uses the most likely amount, which suits a contract with only two possible outcomes.

questions.q: Underhill Corp. sells equipment for $10,500, including a 3-year extended warranty that customers can buy separately. The standalone selling prices are $10,000 for the equipment and $1,200 for the extended warranty. How much revenue should Underhill recognize when the equipment is delivered?
questions.exp: An extended warranty sold separately is a service-type warranty and a separate performance obligation, so the price is allocated by relative standalone prices: $10,500 x 10,000/11,200 = $9,375. The $9,300 answer subtracts the full warranty price as a residual, which does not allocate the bundle discount proportionately.

questions.q: Vance Stores sells $100,000 of gift cards and expects, based on reliable history, that 10% will never be redeemed. During the year customers redeem $45,000 of the cards. Vance has no legal obligation to remit unredeemed amounts to a government. What total revenue should Vance recognize for the year?
questions.exp: Expected breakage is recognized in proportion to the pattern of rights exercised: redemptions are $45,000 of the $90,000 expected, or 50%, so breakage of $10,000 x 50% = $5,000 is added to the $45,000, for $50,000. The $55,000 answer recognizes all breakage at once instead of as redemptions occur.

questions.q: Wexford Co. delivers goods under an agreement that fails the ASC 606 contract criteria because collection is not probable. Wexford receives a $10,000 nonrefundable deposit but has remaining obligations and the contract has not been terminated. How should Wexford account for the deposit?
choices: Recognize revenue in proportion to goods delivered
Offset the deposit against bad debt expense
Record $10,000 as a liability until a revenue event occurs
questions.exp: When a contract fails Step 1, cash received is a liability until a specified event occurs, such as the entity having no remaining obligations, the contract being terminated, or control having transferred with delivery stopped and the cash nonrefundable. Recognizing revenue on receipt ignores the remaining obligations.

questions.q: Which situation requires a performance obligation to be satisfied over time under ASC 606?
choices: The asset has no alternative use and the seller has an enforceable right to payment for work to date
The customer pays a nonrefundable deposit before production begins
Production takes more than one year to complete
The seller retains legal title until the customer pays in full
questions.exp: One of the three over-time criteria is that performance creates an asset with no alternative use to the entity and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date. A long production period or a deposit alone does not meet any criterion, and retaining title for credit protection does not prevent transfer of control.

questions.q: Ashby Co. budgets second-quarter sales of 50,000 units and third-quarter sales of 60,000 units. Its policy is to hold finished goods equal to 20% of the next quarter's sales, and second-quarter beginning inventory complies with the policy at 10,000 units. How many units should Ashby produce in the second quarter?
questions.exp: Production = budgeted sales + desired ending inventory - beginning inventory = 50,000 + (20% x 60,000) - 10,000 = 52,000. Reversing the inventory adjustments gives 48,000.

questions.q: Bolt Co. plans to produce 52,000 units in Quarter 2 and 58,000 units in Quarter 3; each unit requires 3 pounds of material costing $4 per pound. Desired ending materials inventory is 25% of the next quarter's production needs, and Quarter 2 beginning materials inventory is 39,000 pounds. What is the budgeted cost of Quarter 2 materials purchases?
questions.exp: Pounds needed = 156,000 + (25% x 174,000 = 43,500) - 39,000 = 160,500 pounds x $4 = $642,000. Reversing the inventory adjustments gives 151,500 pounds ($606,000), and $624,000 ignores inventory changes altogether.

questions.q: Cove Co. budgets sales of $200,000 for January, $240,000 for February, and $300,000 for March. Thirty percent of sales are for cash. Credit sales are collected 60% in the month after sale and 38% in the second month after sale; 2% are uncollectible. What are budgeted cash collections for March?
questions.exp: March collections = cash sales $90,000 + February credit ($168,000 x 60% = $100,800) + January credit ($140,000 x 38% = $53,200) = $244,000. Applying collection percentages to total sales instead of credit sales gives $310,000.

questions.q: Drake Co. purchases inventory of $400,000 in April and $500,000 in May. It pays 40% of purchases in the month of purchase, taking a 2% discount, and the remaining 60% in the following month. What are Drake's budgeted cash payments for purchases in May?

Elkin Co. expects to begin March with cash of $30,000, collect $420,000, and disburse $480,000 during the month. It must maintain a minimum cash balance of $25,000 and can borrow only in multiples of $10,000. How much should Elkin plan to borrow in March?
questions.exp: Projected balance = $30,000 + $420,000 - $480,000 = $(30,000); reaching the $25,000 minimum requires $55,000, rounded up to the next $10,000 multiple, $60,000. Borrowing only the $30,000 deficit ignores the minimum balance requirement.

questions.q: Ferris Co.'s static budget for 10,000 units showed revenue of $500,000, variable costs of $300,000, and fixed costs of $120,000. Actual results for 11,000 units were revenue of $561,000, variable costs of $341,000, and fixed costs of $125,000. What is Ferris's flexible budget variance for operating income?
questions.exp: Flexible budget at 11,000 units: $550,000 - $330,000 - $120,000 = $100,000; actual income = $95,000, so the flexible budget variance is $5,000 unfavorable. Comparing actual to the static budget ($80,000) mixes in the $20,000 favorable sales-volume effect.

questions.q: Gentry Co. budgeted sales of 20,000 units at $30 per unit with variable costs of $18 per unit. Actual sales were 18,500 units. What is Gentry's sales volume variance measured in contribution margin?
questions.exp: Sales volume variance = (18,500 - 20,000) x budgeted unit CM of $12 = $18,000 unfavorable. Using the selling price ($45,000) measures the revenue effect, not the effect on contribution margin.

questions.q: Hart Co. purchased 12,000 pounds of material for $57,600 and used 10,500 pounds to produce 5,000 units. The standard is 2 pounds per unit at $5.00 per pound. Hart recognizes price variances at the time of purchase. What is the materials price variance?
questions.exp: Actual price = $57,600 / 12,000 = $4.80; price variance = 12,000 x ($5.00 - $4.80) = $2,400 favorable. Computing it on pounds used ($2,100) is appropriate only when price variances are isolated at usage.

questions.q: Ivey Co. produced 5,600 units with a standard of 1.5 direct labor hours per unit at $22.00 per hour. Actual labor was 8,200 hours costing $176,300. What is the direct labor efficiency variance?
questions.exp: Standard hours allowed = 5,600 x 1.5 = 8,400; efficiency variance = (8,200 - 8,400) x $22.00 = $4,400 favorable. Using the actual rate of $21.50 gives $4,300, and $4,100 is the rate variance.

questions.q: Jarvis Co.'s standard is 4 kilograms of material per unit at $2.50 per kilogram. It purchased 14,000 kilograms at $2.40 and used 12,600 kilograms to produce 3,000 units. What is the materials quantity (usage) variance?
questions.exp: Quantity variance = (12,600 - 12,000) x $2.50 standard price = $1,500 unfavorable. Using the actual price ($1,440) is wrong because quantity variances are priced at standard, and using kilograms purchased gives $5,000.

questions.q: Keene Co. applies variable overhead at $6 per direct labor hour, with a standard of 2 hours per unit. It produced 4,000 units using 8,300 actual hours and incurred actual variable overhead of $51,000. What is the variable overhead spending variance?
questions.exp: Spending variance = actual VOH - (actual hours x standard rate) = $51,000 - $49,800 = $1,200 unfavorable. The $1,800 unfavorable figure is the efficiency variance [(8,300 - 8,000) x $6], and $3,000 is the total.

questions.q: Lyle Co. budgeted fixed overhead of $240,000 based on a denominator of 60,000 machine hours. Standard hours allowed for actual output were 57,000, and actual fixed overhead was $246,000. What is the fixed overhead production-volume variance?
questions.exp: Rate = $4 per hour; volume variance = budgeted $240,000 - applied (57,000 x $4 = $228,000) = $12,000 unfavorable, reflecting underuse of capacity. The $6,000 unfavorable figure is the spending variance.

questions.q: Monroe Co. budgeted a unit sales mix of 60% Product A (CM $20) and 40% Product B (CM $10). Actual sales were 5,000 units of A and 5,000 units of B. What is the sales mix variance?
questions.exp: Mix variance = sum of (actual mix % - budgeted mix %) x actual total units x budgeted unit CM: A (50% - 60%) x 10,000 x $20 = $(20,000); B (50% - 40%) x 10,000 x $10 = $10,000; net $10,000 unfavorable. Looking only at Product A gives $20,000.

questions.q: Nolan Co.'s plan called for selling 9,000 units in total, with a budgeted weighting of 60% deluxe models earning $20 each and 40% standard models earning $10 each. Overall volume came in at 10,000 units. How much did the higher total volume, holding the planned weighting constant, change contribution margin?
questions.exp: Budgeted weighted-average CM = (0.6 x $20) + (0.4 x $10) = $16; quantity variance = (10,000 - 9,000) x $16 = $16,000 favorable. Using a simple average CM of $15 ignores the budgeted mix.

questions.q: Oriel Co. budgeted a 10% share of a 200,000-unit market with a budgeted contribution margin of $15 per unit. The actual market was 180,000 units, and Oriel captured a 12% share. What is the market share variance?
questions.exp: Market share variance = (12% - 10%) x actual market of 180,000 x $15 = $54,000 favorable. Using the budgeted market size gives $60,000; the $30,000 unfavorable figure is the market size variance.

questions.q: Pruett Co.'s standard mix for a 100-pound batch is 70 pounds of X at $2 and 30 pounds of Y at $5. During the month it used 6,500 pounds of X and 3,500 pounds of Y. What is the materials mix variance?
questions.exp: At the standard mix, 10,000 pounds would include 7,000 X and 3,000 Y: X (6,500 - 7,000) x $2 = $1,000 favorable; Y (3,500 - 3,000) x $5 = $2,500 unfavorable; net $1,500 unfavorable. Ignoring the favorable X component gives $2,500 unfavorable.

questions.q: Quade Co.'s standard is that 100 pounds of input, costing an average of $2.90 per pound at the standard mix, yields 80 pounds of output. During the month 10,000 pounds of input produced 7,800 pounds of output. What is the materials yield variance?
questions.exp: Standard input for actual output = 7,800 / 0.80 = 9,750 pounds; yield variance = (10,000 - 9,750) x $2.90 = $725 unfavorable. Pricing the 200-pound output shortfall at the input price ($580) misses the 80% yield conversion.

questions.q: Rourke Co.'s overhead cost formula is $45,000 per month plus $3 per machine hour; its static budget assumed 15,000 machine hours. Actual machine hours were 14,000 and actual overhead was $89,500. What is the flexible budget (spending) variance?
questions.exp: Flexible budget at 14,000 hours = $45,000 + $42,000 = $87,000, so the variance is $2,500 unfavorable. Comparing to the static budget of $90,000 shows a misleading $500 favorable result because activity was lower than planned.

questions.q: Sutton Co. collects sales 40% in the month of sale, 50% in the following month, and 10% in the second month after sale. November sales are $300,000 and December sales are $360,000. What is the budgeted accounts receivable balance at December 31?
questions.exp: Uncollected at year-end: 60% of December ($216,000) plus 10% of November ($30,000) = $246,000. Including only December's balance ($216,000) forgets November's final 10%.

questions.q: A city's new manager requires every department to justify all of its proposed spending each year as if the program were starting fresh, rather than adjusting the prior year's amounts. Which budgeting approach is the manager using?
questions.exp: Zero-based budgeting starts each budget at zero and requires justification of every expenditure. Incremental budgeting, the approach being abandoned, adjusts the prior year's base.

questions.q: Taft Co. lets division managers set their own cost budgets, and their bonuses depend on beating those budgets. Managers have consistently overstated expected costs. What is the primary risk this illustrates?
questions.exp: When managers participate in setting the targets they are evaluated against, they may build in slack by overstating costs or understating revenue. Goal congruence is the desired outcome that slack undermines, not the risk itself.

questions.q: Upton Co.'s total direct labor variance was $3,000 unfavorable, including a $5,000 favorable efficiency variance. Workers worked 10,000 actual hours, and the standard rate is $20.00 per hour. What was the actual hourly wage rate?
questions.exp: Rate variance = total - efficiency = $3,000 U - $5,000 F = $8,000 unfavorable, or $0.80 per hour above standard, so the actual rate is $20.80. Dividing the total variance by hours ($20.30) ignores the efficiency component.

questions.q: Vale Co. budgets March manufacturing overhead of $150,000, including $30,000 of depreciation. It pays 80% of cash overhead costs in the month incurred and 20% in the following month. February cash overhead costs were $110,000. What are budgeted cash disbursements for overhead in March?
questions.exp: March cash overhead = $150,000 - $30,000 = $120,000; disbursements = (80% x $120,000) + (20% x $110,000) = $96,000 + $22,000 = $118,000. Including depreciation in the 80% portion gives $142,000.

questions.q: To cut costs, Wiley Co.'s purchasing manager bought lower-grade raw materials at a significant discount. Production then reported higher scrap and longer processing times. Who is most likely responsible for the resulting unfavorable materials quantity and labor efficiency variances?
choices: The production supervisor, because usage variances are always production's responsibility
The purchasing manager, because the low-grade materials caused the excess usage
Nobody, because the favorable price variance offsets them
The human resources manager, because labor efficiency variances relate to wage rates
questions.exp: Variances should be traced to the decision that caused them; here the purchasing choice produced the favorable price variance and the unfavorable usage and efficiency variances. Assigning usage variances to production by default ignores the root cause.

questions.q: Ward Co.'s overhead budget is $60,000 of fixed overhead plus $4 per direct labor hour, with a denominator of 30,000 hours. Actual overhead was $162,000, actual hours were 25,000, and standard hours allowed for actual output were 24,000. Using two-variance analysis, what is the controllable (budget) variance?
questions.exp: Flexible budget at standard hours = $60,000 + (24,000 x $4) = $156,000; controllable variance = $162,000 - $156,000 = $6,000 unfavorable. Using actual hours ($160,000) gives the three-way spending variance of $2,000, and $12,000 is the volume variance.

questions.q: A department's static budget for 10,000 units is $100,000: $60,000 variable ($6 per unit) and $40,000 fixed. The department actually produced 12,000 units and incurred costs of $112,000. What is the department's flexible budget cost variance?
