questions.exp: Flexible budget = (12,000 x $6) + $40,000 = $112,000, equal to actual costs, so there is no flexible budget variance. The $12,000 unfavorable result compares actual costs to the static budget and penalizes the manager for higher volume.

questions.q: Yorke Co. budgeted sales of 10,000 units at $50 each. It actually sold 9,000 units for total revenue of $423,000. What is the sales price variance?
questions.exp: Actual price = $423,000 / 9,000 = $47; price variance = 9,000 x ($47 - $50) = $27,000 unfavorable. Using budgeted units ($30,000) is wrong because the price variance is based on actual units sold.

questions.q: Zeal Co. uses kaizen budgeting and assumes production costs will decline 1% each month from the prior month's budget. January's budgeted cost is $200,000. What is the budgeted cost for March?
questions.exp: Each month is 99% of the prior month: $200,000 x 0.99 x 0.99 = $196,020. A straight-line 1% reduction from January ($196,000) ignores compounding.

questions.q: Abbott Co. plans to produce 20,000 units in Quarter 1 and 24,000 units in Quarter 2. Each unit requires 0.5 direct labor hours. The wage rate is $20 per hour in Quarter 1 and will increase 5% at the start of Quarter 2. What is budgeted direct labor cost for the two quarters combined?
questions.exp: Quarter 1: 10,000 hours x $20 = $200,000; Quarter 2: 12,000 hours x $21 = $252,000; total $452,000. Applying the raise to both quarters gives $462,000, and ignoring it gives $440,000.

questions.q: Benson Co.'s cash budget shows a $100,000 loan at 12% annual interest taken on March 1, with principal and interest repaid together on May 31. What total cash repayment should the May budget show?
questions.exp: Interest = $100,000 x 12% x 3/12 = $3,000, so repayment is $103,000. Using a full year of interest ($112,000) ignores that the loan is outstanding only three months.

questions.q: Carlin Co. uses standard costing and records price variances at purchase. It bought 8,000 pounds of material on account at $3.10 per pound; the standard price is $3.00. What amount should be debited to raw materials inventory?
questions.exp: Raw materials are carried at actual quantity x standard price = 8,000 x $3.00 = $24,000, with an $800 unfavorable price variance debited and accounts payable credited for $24,800. Debiting inventory at actual cost defeats standard costing.

questions.q: Delmont Co. is setting labor standards. Management wants standards that allow for normal machine downtime and worker rest but are still challenging, so that variances signal real problems and employees stay motivated. Which type of standard fits this objective?
questions.exp: Practical standards allow for normal inefficiencies yet are achievable with efficient effort, which supports motivation and meaningful variance analysis. Ideal standards assume perfect conditions and tend to produce chronic unfavorable variances that discourage workers.

questions.q: Ellery Co. budgets setup costs at $500 per batch, with a standard of 200 units per batch. It produced 24,000 units in 110 batches and incurred actual setup costs of $57,000. What is the setup cost spending variance?
questions.exp: Spending variance = actual cost - (actual batches x budgeted rate) = $57,000 - (110 x $500) = $2,000 unfavorable. The $5,000 favorable figure is the efficiency variance [(110 - 120) x $500], and $3,000 favorable is the total flexible budget variance.

questions.q: Fulton Co. begins the year with accounts receivable of $80,000, budgets credit sales of $500,000 and write-offs of uncollectible accounts of $5,000, and expects ending receivables of $95,000. What are budgeted cash collections from customers?
questions.exp: Collections = $80,000 + $500,000 - $5,000 write-offs - $95,000 = $480,000. Ignoring write-offs gives $485,000, overstating cash because written-off accounts are never collected.

questions.q: Gale Co. applies variable overhead at $5 per machine hour with a standard of 0.5 machine hours per unit. It produced 9,000 units using 4,800 machine hours. What is the variable overhead efficiency variance?
questions.exp: Standard hours allowed = 9,000 x 0.5 = 4,500; efficiency variance = (4,800 - 4,500) x $5 = $1,500 unfavorable. Using more hours than allowed is unfavorable, so a favorable label reverses the sign.

questions.q: Each unit of Harlan Co.'s product requires 4.5 pounds of good material, and 10% of material input is normally lost in processing. Material costs $2.00 per pound less a 2% purchase discount, plus $0.10 per pound of freight. What is the standard direct materials cost per unit?
questions.exp: Standard quantity = 4.5 / 0.90 = 5.0 pounds; standard price = $2.00 - $0.04 + $0.10 = $2.06; standard cost = 5.0 x $2.06 = $10.30. Grossing up by 10% of output (4.95 pounds) instead of dividing by 90% gives $10.20.

questions.q: Iverson Co. purchased 20,000 kilograms of material at $3.30 and used 15,000 kilograms; the standard price is $3.50, and the standard quantity allowed for actual output was 14,200 kilograms. Iverson isolates the price variance when materials are used. What is the total direct materials variance for the period?
questions.exp: Price variance at usage = 15,000 x $0.20 = $3,000 favorable; quantity variance = 800 x $3.50 = $2,800 unfavorable; net $200 favorable. Computing the price variance on all 20,000 kilograms purchased gives $1,200 favorable, which is inconsistent with isolating it at usage.

questions.q: Jensen Co., a retailer, budgets April sales of $400,000 and May sales of $480,000. Cost of goods sold is 60% of sales, and desired ending inventory is 25% of the next month's cost of goods sold. April's beginning inventory is $60,000. What are budgeted April merchandise purchases?
questions.exp: Purchases = April COGS $240,000 + ending inventory (25% x $288,000 = $72,000) - beginning $60,000 = $252,000. Reversing the inventory adjustments gives $228,000.

questions.q: During the year, Parker Corp. sold goods that cost it $80,000 to its wholly owned subsidiary, Sloane Co., for $100,000. At year-end, Sloane still holds 30% of these goods. What unrealized profit must be eliminated from consolidated inventory?
questions.exp: Unrealized profit is the intercompany gross profit on goods still held: ($100,000 - $80,000) x 30% = $6,000. The $20,000 answer eliminates profit on the 70% of goods already sold to outsiders, which is realized.

questions.q: Parker Corp. reports sales of $1,000,000, including $100,000 to its subsidiary Sloane Co., and cost of goods sold of $600,000, including $80,000 for the goods sold to Sloane. Sloane reports cost of goods sold of $250,000, which includes $70,000 for 70% of the goods bought from Parker; the rest are in ending inventory. What is consolidated cost of goods sold?
questions.exp: Combined cost of goods sold of $850,000 is reduced by the $100,000 intercompany sale and increased by the $6,000 unrealized profit in ending inventory ($20,000 x 30%): $850,000 - $100,000 + $6,000 = $756,000. The $744,000 answer subtracts the unrealized profit instead of adding it back.

questions.q: Thatcher Co. owns 80% of Ulrich Inc. During the year, Ulrich sold inventory to Thatcher at a profit, and $10,000 of that profit remains unrealized at year-end. Ulrich's reported net income is $200,000. What net income should be attributed to the noncontrolling interest?
questions.exp: In an upstream sale the subsidiary earned the profit, so the elimination is shared with the noncontrolling interest: ($200,000 - $10,000) x 20% = $38,000. The $40,000 answer ignores the unrealized profit, which is correct only for downstream sales.

questions.q: A parent holds an 80% stake in its subsidiary, Walsh Co., which reported earnings of $200,000 this year. The parent made downstream inventory sales to Walsh, leaving $10,000 of intercompany profit in Walsh's year-end stock. What is the outside shareholders' share of consolidated income?
questions.exp: In a downstream sale the parent earned the profit, so the entire elimination is charged to the parent and the noncontrolling interest's share is $200,000 x 20% = $40,000. The $38,000 answer wrongly allocates part of the parent's unrealized profit to the noncontrolling interest.

questions.q: Abbot Corp. sold land costing $50,000 to its subsidiary for $80,000 in Year 1. In Year 3 the subsidiary sells the land to an outside party for $95,000. What gain on the land should the consolidated income statement report in Year 3?
questions.exp: The $30,000 intercompany gain was deferred in consolidation until the land was sold outside the group, so in Year 3 the consolidated gain is the outside price less the group's original cost: $95,000 - $50,000 = $45,000. The $15,000 answer is only the subsidiary's own gain.

questions.q: On January 1, Year 1, Benton Corp. sold equipment with a carrying amount of $60,000 to its wholly owned subsidiary for $90,000. The equipment has a remaining life of 5 years and no salvage value. By how much must Year 1 consolidated net income be reduced relative to the sum of the two companies' separate incomes?
questions.exp: The $30,000 intercompany gain is eliminated, and the excess depreciation of $30,000 / 5 = $6,000 recorded by the subsidiary is reversed, for a net reduction of $30,000 - $6,000 = $24,000. The $30,000 answer forgets that the subsidiary depreciates the inflated cost.

questions.q: Cole Corp.'s subsidiary has bonds payable with a carrying amount of $980,000 held by outside investors. Cole buys all of these bonds on the open market for $950,000. What should the consolidated income statement report for this transaction?
choices: A $50,000 gain based on the bonds' face value
A $30,000 gain on constructive retirement of debt
A $30,000 loss on constructive retirement of debt
No gain or loss until the bonds mature
questions.exp: From the group's perspective, the debt is retired when the parent buys it from outsiders, so the consolidated statements report a gain of $980,000 - $950,000 = $30,000. Deferring the gain until maturity ignores that the group has extinguished its external debt.

questions.q: Drake Co. owns 80% of Ellis Inc. Ellis declares and pays $50,000 of dividends during the year. How do these dividends affect consolidated equity?
questions.exp: The $40,000 paid to Drake is intercompany and eliminated, while the $10,000 paid to outside shareholders (20% x $50,000) reduces the noncontrolling interest. Only the parent's own dividends reduce consolidated retained earnings.

questions.q: Foster Corp. owns 90% of Grant Co. Foster sells 10% of Grant's shares to outside investors for $600,000, keeping control. The carrying amount of Grant's net assets in the consolidated statements, including goodwill, is $5,000,000. How should Foster account for the sale?
choices: Recognize a $100,000 gain in other comprehensive income
questions.exp: A change in ownership that does not cause loss of control is an equity transaction: the noncontrolling interest increases by 10% x $5,000,000 = $500,000, and the $100,000 excess of cash received is credited to additional paid-in capital. No gain is recognized in earnings while control is kept.

questions.q: Hollis Corp. owns 80% of Irwin Co. The carrying amount of Irwin's net assets in consolidation is $1,000,000 and the noncontrolling interest is $200,000. Hollis sells 60% of Irwin's shares for $900,000, losing control; its retained 20% has a fair value of $300,000. What gain should Hollis recognize on deconsolidation?
questions.exp: The gain is the consideration plus the fair value of the retained interest plus the noncontrolling interest, less the subsidiary's net assets: $900,000 + $300,000 + $200,000 - $1,000,000 = $400,000. The $300,000 answer compares the price only with 60% of net assets and ignores the remeasurement of the retained interest.

questions.q: Where should the noncontrolling interest be reported in the consolidated balance sheet?
choices: In equity, separately from the parent's equity
In the mezzanine section for all companies
As a reduction of the parent's total assets
As a liability between current and long-term debt
questions.exp: ASC 810 requires the noncontrolling interest to be reported within equity, clearly identified and separate from the parent's equity. Mezzanine presentation applies only to certain redeemable noncontrolling interests of SEC registrants, not to all companies.

questions.q: Kirby Co. owns 70% of Lowe Inc., which has incurred losses large enough that the noncontrolling interest's share would create a deficit balance. How should Kirby attribute the further losses?
choices: Attribute losses to the noncontrolling interest only up to its investment
Continue attributing 30% to the noncontrolling interest, even if it becomes a deficit
Attribute all further losses to the parent
Stop recording losses until profits resume
questions.exp: Losses attributable to the noncontrolling interest continue to be attributed to it even if that results in a deficit balance (ASC 810-10-45-21). Charging excess losses to the parent was the treatment before the 2009 standard took effect.

questions.q: Which characteristic causes a legal entity to be a variable interest entity?
choices: The entity is financed partly with long-term debt
The entity has more than one class of voting stock
Its equity at risk is not enough to finance its activities without additional subordinated support
The entity's shares are not publicly traded
questions.exp: An entity is a VIE if its equity investment at risk is insufficient to finance its activities without additional subordinated financial support, or if its equity holders as a group lack power, the obligation to absorb losses or the right to receive residual returns. Ordinary debt financing or multiple classes of stock do not by themselves create a VIE.

questions.q: Which entity is the primary beneficiary of a variable interest entity?
choices: The entity that absorbs the majority of expected losses, regardless of power
The entity that holds the largest share of the VIE's voting equity
The entity with power over the most significant activities and significant exposure to losses or benefits
The entity that provides the largest amount of debt financing
questions.exp: The primary beneficiary has both the power to direct the activities that most significantly affect the VIE's economic performance and the obligation to absorb losses or the right to receive benefits that could be significant to the VIE. The majority-of-expected-losses test was replaced by this qualitative power and economics model.

questions.q: Marsh Advisors manages an investment fund that is a VIE and earns a fee that is customary and commensurate with the services provided. Marsh holds no other interest in the fund. Is Marsh's fee a variable interest?
choices: No, but Marsh still consolidates because it has power
Yes, because Marsh has power over the fund
Yes, because any fee that varies with performance is a variable interest
No, so Marsh is not the primary beneficiary
questions.exp: A decision maker's fee is not a variable interest if it is customary and commensurate with the services and the decision maker holds no other interests that would absorb more than an insignificant amount of variability. Without a variable interest, Marsh cannot be the primary beneficiary, even though it has power.

questions.q: Norton Co. designs and manages a leasing entity under a contract that cannot be terminated, and it guarantees all of the entity's debt. An outside investor holds all of the entity's equity, which is 3% of total assets and has no say over operations. Which party should consolidate the leasing entity?
choices: The outside investor, as the sole equity holder
Neither party, because the entity is independent
questions.exp: The entity is a VIE because its equity is thin and its equity holder lacks power, and Norton both directs the most significant activities and absorbs potentially significant losses through the guarantee, so Norton is the primary beneficiary. Holding 100% of the equity does not mean control when the equity holder has no power.

questions.q: How often must a reporting entity reassess whether it is the primary beneficiary of a VIE?
choices: Only at the inception of its involvement
Only when the VIE issues new equity
questions.exp: ASC 810-10-35-4 requires the primary beneficiary determination to be assessed continuously, because power and economics can shift. By contrast, whether an entity is a VIE is reconsidered only when specified reconsideration events occur.

questions.q: Oakes Corp. becomes the primary beneficiary of a VIE that is not a business, and the two are not under common control. How does Oakes initially measure the VIE's assets and liabilities?
choices: At the lower of carrying amount or fair value
At fair value, recognizing any difference as a gain or loss with no goodwill
At fair value, recognizing goodwill for any excess
At the VIE's historical carrying amounts
questions.exp: A primary beneficiary initially measures the assets, liabilities and noncontrolling interest of a VIE at fair value; when the VIE is not a business, no goodwill is recognized and any difference is a gain or loss. Carrying amounts are used only when the parties are under common control.

questions.q: Under ASU 2018-17, which accounting alternative is available to private companies?
choices: Not applying the VIE guidance to certain legal entities under common control
Not consolidating any subsidiary with less than 80% ownership
Using the equity method for all VIEs
questions.exp: Private companies may elect not to apply VIE guidance to legal entities under common control when specified criteria are met, with disclosures instead. They still apply the voting interest model, so subsidiaries they control through voting rights are consolidated.

questions.q: Porter Co. owns 60% of the voting shares of Quill Inc. The minority shareholder has the right to approve Quill's annual operating budget and to select and terminate senior management. How should Porter account for Quill under the voting interest model?
choices: Not consolidate it, because the minority shareholder has substantive participating rights
Not consolidate it unless Porter owns more than 80%
Consolidate it, because Porter has a majority vote
Consolidate it, because these are protective rights
questions.exp: Rights to approve operating budgets and to select and terminate management are substantive participating rights, which overcome the presumption that a majority owner controls; Porter would use the equity method. Protective rights, such as approval of major asset sales, would not prevent consolidation.

questions.q: Reid Corp. acquires 80% of Sterling Co. for $800,000. The fair value of the noncontrolling interest is $200,000. Sterling's book value is $700,000, and its building is worth $200,000 more than book value; there are no other differences. What goodwill should be reported in the consolidated balance sheet?
questions.exp: The fair value of Sterling's identifiable net assets is $700,000 + $200,000 = $900,000, so goodwill is $800,000 + $200,000 - $900,000 = $100,000. The $80,000 answer measures only the parent's share, but US GAAP recognizes goodwill for the whole entity.

questions.q: Using the same facts (Reid acquired 80% of Sterling; the noncontrolling interest's fair value was $200,000 and the building step-up of $200,000 has a 10-year remaining life), Sterling earns net income of $150,000 and pays $40,000 of dividends in Year 1. What is the noncontrolling interest balance at the end of Year 1?
questions.exp: The noncontrolling interest shares income after the extra $20,000 depreciation and its share of dividends: $200,000 + 20% x ($150,000 - $20,000) - 20% x $40,000 = $218,000. The $222,000 answer ignores the depreciation of the building step-up.

questions.q: Tate Corp. lends $500,000 to its wholly owned subsidiary at 6%, and the subsidiary pays $30,000 of interest during the year. What is the net effect of eliminating this interest on consolidated net income?
questions.exp: The elimination removes $30,000 of interest income and $30,000 of interest expense, so consolidated net income is unchanged. Eliminating only the income side would wrongly reduce net income by $30,000.

questions.q: On the date Vale Corp. acquires 100% of Warner Co., Vale's retained earnings are $2,000,000 and Warner's are $600,000. What is consolidated retained earnings at the acquisition date?
questions.exp: A subsidiary's retained earnings at the acquisition date are eliminated against the investment because they were earned before the parent owned it, so consolidated retained earnings equal the parent's $2,000,000. Adding the two balances would include pre-acquisition earnings the group did not earn.

questions.q: Yates Co. sold inventory to its wholly owned subsidiary last year, and $5,000 of unrealized profit was in the subsidiary's ending inventory. The subsidiary sold all of those goods to outsiders this year. How does this affect current-year consolidated net income compared with the companies' separate incomes?
choices: Consolidated net income is higher by $10,000
Consolidated net income is higher by $5,000
Consolidated net income is lower by $5,000
There is no effect in the current year
questions.exp: Profit deferred at the end of last year is realized when the goods are sold to outsiders this year, so the beginning inventory adjustment lowers consolidated cost of goods sold and raises consolidated net income by $5,000. Treating it as having no effect ignores that the deferral reverses.

questions.q: Zeller Corp. accounts for its subsidiary using the equity method on its own books, recording all required adjustments. How does Zeller's separate net income compare with consolidated net income attributable to Zeller?
choices: Zeller's separate net income is lower
Zeller's separate net income is higher
It depends on the noncontrolling interest's share
questions.exp: A fully applied equity method, including amortization of fair value adjustments and elimination of intercompany profits, produces parent net income equal to consolidated net income attributable to the parent; for this reason it is sometimes called a one-line consolidation. Consolidation changes the presentation but not the parent's share of income.

questions.q: In VIE analysis, when are kick-out rights over the decision maker considered in deciding who has power?
choices: Never, because VIE analysis ignores kick-out rights
Whenever any group of investors holds them
Only when a single party, with its related parties, can exercise them unilaterally
Only when they can be exercised by a majority of equity holders
questions.exp: For VIEs, substantive kick-out or participating rights affect the power analysis only when a single variable interest holder, including its related parties, can exercise them unilaterally. Rights that require many unrelated parties to act together are not enough to remove power from the decision maker.

questions.q: Where should dividends paid by a subsidiary to its noncontrolling shareholders be reported in the consolidated statement of cash flows?
choices: They are eliminated and not reported
questions.exp: Dividends paid to noncontrolling shareholders are a distribution to owners of the consolidated group and are reported as financing outflows. Only dividends paid to the parent are intercompany and eliminated.

questions.q: Archer Corp. owns 75% of Bishop Co. Archer's separate income, excluding any income from Bishop, is $400,000, and Bishop's net income is $160,000. At year-end, $12,000 of profit on Bishop's sales to Archer remains unrealized. What consolidated net income is attributable to Archer?
questions.exp: Bishop's income adjusted for the upstream profit is $160,000 - $12,000 = $148,000, of which Archer's 75% is $111,000, so income attributable to Archer is $400,000 + $111,000 = $511,000. The $508,000 answer charges the entire upstream elimination to the parent, which is the downstream treatment.

questions.q: Under ASC 810, what is presumed about an equity investment at risk that is less than 10% of a legal entity's total assets?
choices: It is irrelevant to the VIE analysis
It is presumed insufficient unless shown to be sufficient
It automatically makes the entity a VIE with no rebuttal
It is presumed sufficient if the entity is profitable
questions.exp: ASC 810-10-25-45 presumes that equity at risk below 10% of total assets is insufficient to finance the entity's activities unless sufficiency is demonstrated, for example by showing the entity can obtain non-subordinated financing. The presumption can be rebutted, so it is not automatic, and equity of 10% or more is not automatically sufficient either.

questions.q: Ardent Co. sells a product for $40 per unit with variable costs of $24 per unit. Fixed costs are $480,000 per year. What is Ardent's breakeven point in units?
questions.exp: Breakeven units = fixed costs / unit contribution margin = $480,000 / ($40 - $24) = 30,000. Dividing by variable cost ($24) gives 20,000 and dividing by price gives 12,000.

questions.q: Basin Co. has annual fixed costs of $360,000 and a contribution margin ratio of 30%. What is Basin's breakeven point in sales dollars?
questions.exp: Breakeven sales = $360,000 / 0.30 = $1,200,000. Dividing by the variable cost ratio (0.70) gives $514,286.

questions.q: Crest Co. sells its product for $50 per unit; variable cost is $30 per unit and fixed costs are $200,000. How many units must Crest sell to earn pretax operating income of $100,000?
questions.exp: Required units = ($200,000 + $100,000) / $20 = 15,000. The 10,000 figure is only breakeven, and 6,000 divides by price rather than contribution margin.

questions.q: Delta Co. sells a product for $60 per unit with variable costs of $36 per unit and fixed costs of $240,000. Its income tax rate is 25%. How many units must Delta sell to earn net income of $90,000?
questions.exp: Required pretax income = $90,000 / (1 - 0.25) = $120,000; units = ($240,000 + $120,000) / $24 = 15,000. Using the after-tax target directly gives 13,750.

questions.q: Ember Co. has budgeted sales of $900,000 and breakeven sales of $720,000. What is Ember's margin of safety ratio?
questions.exp: Margin of safety = ($900,000 - $720,000) / $900,000 = 20.0% of budgeted sales. Dividing by breakeven sales instead gives 25.0%.

questions.q: Fable Co. has sales of $1,000,000, variable costs of $600,000, and fixed costs of $300,000. If sales increase by 10% with no change in cost structure, what will operating income be?
questions.exp: Degree of operating leverage = CM / operating income = $400,000 / $100,000 = 4, so a 10% sales increase raises income 40%, to $140,000 (equivalently, CM rises by $40,000). Assuming income grows at the same 10% rate as sales ignores operating leverage.

questions.q: Grove Co. sells Products A and B in a constant unit mix of 3 A to 2 B. Unit contribution margins are $10 for A and $15 for B, and fixed costs are $300,000. How many units of B must be sold to break even?
questions.exp: A package of 3 A and 2 B has CM of $30 + $30 = $60, so breakeven is $300,000 / $60 = 5,000 packages, or 10,000 units of B. Using a simple average CM of $12.50 instead of the mix-weighted $12.00 gives 9,600.

questions.q: Haven Co. sells two products. Product X provides 60% of sales dollars with a 40% contribution margin ratio; Product Y provides 40% of sales dollars with a 25% contribution margin ratio. Fixed costs are $170,000. What are Haven's breakeven sales?
questions.exp: Weighted CM ratio = (0.60 x 40%) + (0.40 x 25%) = 34%; breakeven = $170,000 / 0.34 = $500,000. A simple average CM ratio of 32.5% ignores the sales mix and gives $523,077.

questions.q: Ivory Co. is choosing between two production methods. Method 1 has fixed costs of $200,000 and variable costs of $30 per unit; Method 2 has fixed costs of $350,000 and variable costs of $20 per unit. At what volume are total costs equal?
questions.exp: Set $200,000 + $30Q = $350,000 + $20Q, so $10Q = $150,000 and Q = 15,000 units; above that volume, Method 2 is cheaper. Dividing one method's fixed cost by the other's variable cost (for example, $350,000 / $30) is a common error.

questions.q: Jasper Co. sells 50,000 units at $30 with variable costs of $18 per unit and fixed costs of $400,000. Management proposes cutting the price to $27, which it expects to increase unit sales by 30%. What is the effect of the proposal on operating income?
questions.exp: Current CM = 50,000 x $12 = $600,000; proposed CM = 65,000 x $9 = $585,000; fixed costs are unchanged, so income falls $15,000. Applying the 30% volume increase to the old CM ($180,000 increase) ignores the lower unit margin.

questions.q: Kestrel Co.'s annual fixed costs of $500,000 include $100,000 of depreciation. Unit contribution margin is $20, and all other costs are paid in cash. What is Kestrel's cash breakeven point in units?
questions.exp: Cash breakeven excludes noncash fixed costs: ($500,000 - $100,000) / $20 = 20,000 units. Using total fixed costs gives the accounting breakeven of 25,000 units.

questions.q: Laurel Co. has a contribution margin ratio of 40%. Its fixed costs are expected to increase by $60,000. By how much will Laurel's breakeven sales increase?
questions.exp: Breakeven sales rise by the fixed-cost increase divided by the CM ratio: $60,000 / 0.40 = $150,000. Dividing by the variable cost ratio (0.60) gives $100,000.

questions.q: Maple Co. expects to sell 25,000 units of a new product. Variable cost is $15 per unit and fixed costs are $300,000. What selling price per unit will produce operating income of $200,000?
questions.exp: Price = $15 + ($300,000 + $200,000) / 25,000 = $15 + $20 = $35. Covering only fixed costs ($27) yields breakeven, not the profit target.

questions.q: Which of the following is an underlying assumption of traditional cost-volume-profit analysis?
choices: Inventory levels change significantly from period to period
The sales mix shifts toward higher-margin products as volume increases
Total fixed costs remain constant within the relevant range
Unit variable costs decline as volume increases because of learning effects
questions.exp: CVP assumes linear revenue and cost functions within the relevant range, with constant total fixed costs, constant unit variable cost and price, a constant sales mix, and units produced equal to units sold. Declining unit variable costs would violate the linearity assumption.

questions.q: Nimbus Co. sells a product for $20 with variable costs of $12 per unit and fixed costs of $120,000. What sales revenue is needed to earn operating income equal to 15% of sales?
questions.exp: CM ratio = 40%; 0.40S - $120,000 = 0.15S, so 0.25S = $120,000 and S = $480,000. Dividing fixed costs by 0.55 (adding the margin to the CM ratio rather than subtracting) gives $218,182.

questions.q: Orchid Co.'s margin of safety is 25% of current sales. If sales decline by 10% and the cost structure is unchanged, by what percentage will operating income decline?
questions.exp: Degree of operating leverage = 1 / margin of safety ratio = 1 / 0.25 = 4, so income falls 4 x 10% = 40%. Assuming income changes in proportion to sales gives 10%.

questions.q: Pinnacle Co. sells a product for $50 with variable costs of $30 per unit. Fixed costs are $260,000 for volumes up to 12,000 units and $320,000 for volumes from 12,001 to 20,000 units. What is Pinnacle's breakeven point?
questions.exp: At the lower step, breakeven would be $260,000 / $20 = 13,000 units, which is outside that step's 12,000-unit range; at the higher step, $320,000 / $20 = 16,000 units, which falls within its range. The 13,000 answer ignores that fixed costs step up above 12,000 units.

questions.q: Quarry Co. sells a product for $40; fixed costs are $480,000. Variable costs are expected to rise from $24 to $26 per unit. What will Quarry's breakeven point be after the increase?
questions.exp: New unit CM = $40 - $26 = $14; breakeven = $480,000 / $14 = 34,286 units (rounded). Dividing fixed costs by the new variable cost gives 18,462, and 30,000 is the old breakeven.

questions.q: Ridge Co. sells Product A (CM $20) and Product B (CM $8); fixed costs are $240,000. The unit sales mix is expected to shift from 50% A / 50% B to 25% A / 75% B. What is Ridge's total breakeven volume in units under the new mix?
questions.exp: New weighted CM = (0.25 x $20) + (0.75 x $8) = $11; breakeven = $240,000 / $11 = 21,818 units. The old mix ($14 weighted CM) gives 17,143, so shifting toward the lower-margin product raises breakeven.

questions.q: Sable Co. has sales of $800,000, a contribution margin ratio of 35%, fixed costs of $210,000, and an income tax rate of 21%. What is Sable's net income?
questions.exp: Operating income = ($800,000 x 0.35) - $210,000 = $70,000; net income = $70,000 x (1 - 0.21) = $55,300. The $70,000 choice omits income taxes.

questions.q: Tundra Co. breaks even at 8,000 units. Its fixed costs are $240,000 and its selling price is $75 per unit. What is Tundra's variable cost per unit?
questions.exp: Unit CM = $240,000 / 8,000 = $30, so variable cost = $75 - $30 = $45. The $30 figure is the contribution margin, not the variable cost.

questions.q: Two companies each have sales of $1,000,000 and operating income of $100,000. Highland Co. has variable costs of $300,000 and fixed costs of $600,000; Lowland Co. has variable costs of $700,000 and fixed costs of $200,000. If both companies' sales increase by 10%, what will Highland's operating income be?
questions.exp: Highland's DOL = $700,000 / $100,000 = 7, so a 10% sales increase raises income 70%, to $170,000 (CM grows by $70,000). The $130,000 amount is Lowland's result with a DOL of 3.

questions.q: Umbra Co. sells a product for $25 per unit. Variable manufacturing cost is $10 per unit and sales commissions are 10% of the selling price. Fixed costs are $180,000. What is Umbra's breakeven point in units?
questions.exp: Unit CM = $25 - $10 - $2.50 commission = $12.50; breakeven = $180,000 / $12.50 = 14,400 units. Omitting the commission (CM of $15) gives 12,000 units.

questions.q: Vista Co. sells a product for $30 with variable costs of $18 per unit and fixed costs of $120,000. How many units must Vista sell to earn operating income of $4 per unit sold?
questions.exp: Treat the per-unit profit like a variable cost: ($30 - $18 - $4)Q = $120,000, so Q = 15,000 units. Adding the $4 to CM ($16) gives 7,500, which moves the target the wrong direction.

questions.q: Willow Co. has a contribution margin ratio of 30%. A proposed $45,000 advertising campaign is expected to increase sales by $120,000. What is the effect of the campaign on operating income?
questions.exp: Incremental CM = $120,000 x 30% = $36,000, less the $45,000 cost, a $9,000 decrease. Subtracting the cost from incremental sales rather than incremental CM gives $75,000.

questions.q: Xenon Co. has a 45% contribution margin ratio before sales compensation and fixed costs of $500,000 excluding sales staff. It can pay its sales staff fixed salaries totaling $300,000 or commissions of 15% of sales. At what sales level would operating income be the same under both plans?
questions.exp: Salary plan: 0.45S - $800,000; commission plan: 0.30S - $500,000. Setting them equal gives 0.15S = $300,000, so S = $2,000,000. Dividing $500,000 by the 30% CM ratio gives only the commission plan's breakeven.

questions.q: Yarrow Co. earned operating income of $20,000 on sales of $400,000 and $60,000 on sales of $500,000, with no change in prices, unit costs, or fixed costs. What is Yarrow's breakeven sales volume?
questions.exp: CM ratio = $40,000 / $100,000 = 40%; fixed costs = (0.40 x $400,000) - $20,000 = $140,000; breakeven = $140,000 / 0.40 = $350,000. Subtracting income from sales ($380,000) is not a breakeven calculation.

questions.q: Zephyr Co.'s pretax breakeven point is 20,000 units. If its income tax rate increases from 21% to 30%, what will its breakeven point be?
questions.exp: At breakeven there is no taxable income, so the tax rate does not affect breakeven: it remains 20,000 units. Grossing up the breakeven volume by the tax rate confuses breakeven with an after-tax profit target.

questions.q: Aspen Co. sells Products X and Y in a 2-to-1 unit mix. X sells for $30 with variable cost of $20; Y sells for $50 with variable cost of $35. Fixed costs are $420,000. What are Aspen's breakeven sales in dollars?
questions.exp: A composite unit (2 X + 1 Y) has CM of $20 + $15 = $35 and revenue of $60 + $50 = $110; breakeven = $420,000 / $35 = 12,000 composites x $110 = $1,320,000. Ignoring the 2-to-1 mix (CM of $25 per composite) produces $1,848,000.

questions.q: Birch Co. sells 20,000 units at $50 with variable costs of $30 per unit and fixed costs of $200,000. Automation would raise fixed costs by $40,000 and cut variable costs to $26 per unit. How many units must Birch sell after automating to keep operating income at its current level?
questions.exp: Current income = 20,000 x $20 - $200,000 = $200,000; required units = ($240,000 + $200,000) / $24 = 18,333. The 10,000 figure is the new breakeven, not the volume that preserves current profit.

questions.q: Cedar Co. sells 10,000 units at $80 with variable costs of $50 per unit and fixed costs of $200,000. What is Cedar's degree of operating leverage at this volume?
questions.exp: CM = 10,000 x $30 = $300,000; operating income = $100,000; DOL = $300,000 / $100,000 = 3.0. Dividing CM by fixed costs (1.5) uses the wrong denominator.

questions.q: Dover Co. sold 10,000 units for $500,000. Its absorption-costing statement shows COGS of $300,000, including $100,000 of fixed manufacturing overhead, and selling and administrative expenses of $150,000, including $50,000 of variable costs. Inventory levels did not change. What is Dover's breakeven point in units?
questions.exp: Variable cost per unit = ($200,000 + $50,000) / 10,000 = $25, so CM = $25; fixed costs = $100,000 + $100,000 = $200,000; breakeven = 8,000 units. Using gross margin per unit ($20) and treating all S&A as fixed gives 7,500, mixing fixed and variable costs.

questions.q: Elm Co. has a 40% contribution margin ratio. Variable cost per unit will rise from $24 to $27. What selling price will maintain the 40% contribution margin ratio?
questions.exp: Variable costs must remain 60% of price: $27 / 0.60 = $45.00. Passing through only the $3 cost increase ($43.00) lets the CM ratio fall, and dividing by 0.40 confuses the CM ratio with the variable cost ratio.

questions.q: Fern Co. sells a product for $40 with variable costs of $28 per unit and fixed costs of $360,000. Budgeted sales are 36,000 units. What is Fern's margin of safety in sales dollars?
questions.exp: Breakeven = $360,000 / $12 = 30,000 units; margin of safety = 6,000 units x $40 = $240,000. Multiplying the 6,000 units by CM ($72,000) measures the profit cushion, not sales dollars.

questions.q: In a profit-volume graph with units sold on the horizontal axis and operating income on the vertical axis, what do the slope of the profit line and its vertical-axis intercept represent?
choices: Slope is the unit contribution margin; intercept is negative total fixed costs
Slope is the selling price per unit; intercept is total fixed costs
Slope is the contribution margin ratio; intercept is zero
Slope is the variable cost per unit; intercept is the breakeven volume
questions.exp: Operating income = (unit CM x units) - fixed costs, so the line rises at the unit CM and crosses the vertical axis at a loss equal to fixed costs. Selling price is the slope of the revenue line on a CVP graph, not the profit line.

questions.q: Grey Co. sells a product with a constant contribution margin and fixed costs. If Grey raises its selling price while unit variable costs, fixed costs, and expected unit sales stay the same, what happens to its breakeven point and its margin of safety?
choices: Breakeven decreases; margin of safety decreases
Breakeven increases; margin of safety decreases
Breakeven unchanged; margin of safety increases
Breakeven decreases; margin of safety increases
questions.exp: A higher price raises unit CM, which lowers breakeven units; with expected sales unchanged, the gap between expected and breakeven sales (margin of safety) widens. Candidates sometimes think breakeven is unaffected because fixed costs did not change.

questions.q: Hazel Co. has fixed costs of $300,000, a contribution margin ratio of 25%, and an income tax rate of 20%. What sales are required to earn net income of $60,000?
questions.exp: Pretax target = $60,000 / 0.80 = $75,000; required sales = ($300,000 + $75,000) / 0.25 = $1,500,000. Using the after-tax target directly gives $1,440,000.

questions.q: Iris Co. reports a full cost of $36 per unit at its normal volume of 20,000 units, consisting of $21 variable cost and $15 fixed cost per unit. The selling price is $40. What is Iris's breakeven point in units?
questions.exp: Total fixed costs = $15 x 20,000 = $300,000; unit CM = $40 - $21 = $19; breakeven = $300,000 / $19 = 15,790 units (rounded up). Dividing by the $4 margin over full cost (75,000) wrongly treats unitized fixed cost as variable.

questions.q: A controller builds a dashboard showing last quarter's sales by region, product line and month, compared with the prior year. Which type of analytics does this represent?
questions.exp: Descriptive analytics summarizes what happened using historical data, such as period sales reports and comparisons. It becomes diagnostic only when the analysis drills into why results occurred.

questions.q: After gross margin declined 3 points, an analyst drills down by customer, product and plant and finds that the decline came from scrap at one facility. Which type of analytics is this?
questions.exp: Diagnostic analytics answers why something happened, typically through drill-downs, data discovery and correlation analysis. Simply reporting the 3-point decline would be descriptive; explaining its cause is diagnostic.

questions.q: A lender develops a model that uses payment history, debt levels and industry data to estimate the probability that each borrower will default in the next 12 months. Which type of analytics is this?
questions.exp: Predictive analytics uses historical patterns to estimate what is likely to happen, such as default probabilities. It would be prescriptive only if the model went on to recommend an action, such as which loans to approve or how to price them.

questions.q: A retailer uses an optimization model that considers forecast demand, carrying costs and supplier lead times to recommend the reorder quantity for each item. Which type of analytics is this?
questions.exp: Prescriptive analytics recommends what should be done, often through optimization or simulation. The demand forecast that feeds the model is predictive, but the recommendation of a specific action makes the overall tool prescriptive.

questions.q: A regression of monthly maintenance cost on machine hours gives the equation: cost = $5,000 + $3.20 x machine hours. What is the predicted maintenance cost for a month with 2,000 machine hours?
questions.exp: Predicted cost = $5,000 + $3.20 x 2,000 = $5,000 + $6,400 = $11,400. The $6,400 answer omits the intercept, which represents the estimated fixed cost.

questions.q: The correlation coefficient between advertising spending and monthly sales is 0.90 in a simple linear regression. What does the coefficient of determination indicate?
choices: 81% of the variation in sales is explained by advertising
Each $1 of advertising produces $0.81 of sales
90% of the variation in sales is explained by advertising
questions.exp: In simple regression, R-squared equals the correlation coefficient squared: 0.90 x 0.90 = 0.81, so 81% of the variation in sales is explained. Reading r itself as the explained proportion is the common error, and neither statistic proves causation.

questions.q: In a multiple regression predicting store sales, the coefficient on local population has a p-value of 0.03. Using a 5% significance level, what should the analyst conclude?
choices: The variable should be removed because 0.03 is below 0.05
The model as a whole has a 3% chance of being correct
The coefficient is statistically significant, so the null hypothesis that it equals zero is rejected
The variable explains 97% of the variation in sales
questions.exp: A p-value below the 0.05 significance level means the coefficient is statistically different from zero. The p-value is not a measure of explained variation; that is R-squared.

questions.q: An analyst finds a strong positive correlation between the number of employee training hours and customer complaints across branches. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
choices: Customer complaints cause additional training hours
Training causes customer complaints and should be reduced
The correlation proves a causal link in one direction or the other
The variables are associated, but further analysis is needed because correlation does not establish causation
questions.exp: Correlation measures association only; a third factor such as branch size or new-hire volume could drive both variables. Concluding that one causes the other in either direction is unsupported without further analysis.

questions.q: A multiple regression model uses both square footage and number of rooms to predict office rent. The two independent variables have a correlation of 0.95, and their coefficients have unexpected signs and large standard errors. What problem is most likely present?
questions.exp: Multicollinearity occurs when independent variables are highly correlated, making individual coefficients unstable and imprecise even when the overall model fit is good. Autocorrelation concerns correlated residuals over time, not correlation between predictors.

questions.q: A cost model was estimated from monthly data with production between 2,000 and 6,000 units. Management wants to use it to predict costs for a planned month of 12,000 units. What is the primary concern?
choices: Extrapolating beyond the relevant range may give unreliable predictions because cost behavior may change
Regression models cannot be used for budgeting
The model's R-squared will automatically decline
The intercept must be removed before predicting
questions.exp: A regression describes the relationship only within the range of observed data; outside it, step costs, capacity limits or new shifts may change cost behavior. R-squared describes historical fit and does not change when the model is misapplied.

questions.q: Maintenance cost was $65,000 in the highest-activity month (10,000 units) and $41,000 in the lowest-activity month (4,000 units). Using the high-low method, what are the variable cost per unit and the monthly fixed cost?
questions.exp: Variable cost = ($65,000 - $41,000) / (10,000 - 4,000) = $4.00 per unit; fixed cost = $65,000 - $4.00 x 10,000 = $25,000. The $6.50 answer divides total cost by units and ignores the fixed component.

questions.q: In a regression output, the coefficient on labor hours is 2.5 with a standard error of 0.5. What is the t-statistic, and what does it suggest?
choices: 5.0; the coefficient is likely statistically significant
questions.exp: t = coefficient / standard error = 2.5 / 0.5 = 5.0, well above the rough threshold of 2, so the coefficient is likely significant. The 0.2 answer inverts the ratio.

questions.q: A customer master file lists the same customer three times under slightly different spellings, inflating the active customer count and splitting credit limits. Which data quality dimension is primarily violated?
questions.exp: Uniqueness requires each real-world entity to be recorded once; duplicate records violate it and distort counts and credit monitoring. Completeness concerns missing values, which is not the issue here.

questions.q: The sales system records dates as MM/DD/YYYY and the ERP system records them as DD/MM/YYYY. When the data are merged, many transactions are assigned to the wrong month. Which data quality dimension is most directly at issue?
questions.exp: Consistency requires the same data to be represented the same way across systems; conflicting date formats cause misinterpretation when data are combined. The values exist, so completeness is not the problem.

questions.q: A purchasing team makes daily reorder decisions using an inventory report that is refreshed only once a week. Which data quality dimension is the main weakness?
questions.exp: Timeliness means data are available and current when needed for the decision; weekly data cannot support daily decisions reliably. The report may have been accurate when produced, so accuracy is not the core issue.

questions.q: In an extract, transform, load (ETL) process for a data warehouse, which activity occurs in the transform step?
choices: Cleansing, standardizing formats and applying business rules
Pulling raw records from source systems
Granting user access to the warehouse
Writing the final records to the warehouse tables
questions.exp: The transform step cleanses data, converts formats, removes duplicates and applies business rules before loading. Pulling records is extraction and writing to the warehouse is loading.

questions.q: An audit team wants to analyze vendor contracts stored as PDFs, emails with customers and recordings of call-center conversations. How are these data best classified?
questions.exp: Documents, emails and audio lack a predefined row-and-column format, so they are unstructured and often require text or speech analytics. Structured data reside in fixed fields such as ERP tables.

questions.q: A CFO wants to show the board how monthly revenue has changed over the past 36 months. Which visualization is most appropriate?
questions.exp: Line charts are best for showing trends in a continuous measure over time. Pie charts show composition at a single point and become unreadable with 36 slices.

questions.q: An analyst wants to show whether stores with higher local advertising spending also have higher sales, using data from 50 stores. Which visualization is most appropriate?
questions.exp: A scatter plot displays the relationship between two quantitative variables across observations and reveals correlation and outliers. A line chart implies an ordered sequence such as time, which the store data lack.

questions.q: An internal auditor wants to show how 5,000 expense report amounts are distributed, including clustering just below the $75 receipt threshold. Which visualization is most appropriate?
questions.exp: A histogram groups a single quantitative variable into bins and shows its distribution, making a spike just under $75 visible. A scatter plot needs two variables and would not show frequency as clearly.

questions.q: A bar chart compares on-time delivery rates of 96%, 97% and 98% for three warehouses, with the vertical axis starting at 95%. What is the main concern?
choices: The truncated axis visually exaggerates small differences between warehouses
The axis should start at the lowest value, 96%
The chart should use a pie chart to compare categories
questions.exp: Starting a bar chart's axis well above zero makes a 2-point difference look several times larger than it is, misleading users. Pie charts show parts of a whole and are not suitable for comparing separate rates.

questions.q: A financial model is run under best-case, base-case and worst-case assumptions, with sales volume, selling price and material cost all changed together in each case. What technique is this?
questions.exp: Scenario analysis changes multiple related inputs simultaneously to evaluate coherent alternative futures. Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time while holding the others constant.

questions.q: A project's NPV under three scenarios is: best case $500,000 (30% probability), base case $200,000 (50% probability) and worst case -$300,000 (20% probability). What is the expected NPV?
questions.exp: Expected NPV = 0.30 x $500,000 + 0.50 x $200,000 + 0.20 x (-$300,000) = $150,000 + $100,000 - $60,000 = $190,000. The $133,333 answer is a simple average that ignores the probabilities.

questions.q: A product sells 10,000 units at $50 per unit, with variable costs of $30 per unit and fixed costs of $150,000. In a sensitivity analysis, what is operating income if the selling price falls 10% and all other inputs are unchanged?
questions.exp: Base income is 10,000 x ($50 - $30) - $150,000 = $50,000; at a $45 price, 10,000 x ($45 - $30) - $150,000 = $0. The $45,000 answer simply cuts income by 10%, ignoring operating leverage.

questions.q: How does Monte Carlo simulation differ from basic sensitivity analysis in financial modeling?
choices: It identifies the single optimal decision without considering uncertainty
It uses only best-case and worst-case values
It assigns probability distributions to uncertain inputs and runs many iterations to produce a distribution of possible outcomes
It changes one input at a time by a fixed percentage
questions.exp: Monte Carlo simulation draws random values from input distributions over thousands of trials, producing a probability distribution of outputs. Changing one input at a time describes sensitivity analysis.

questions.q: Five days-to-pay observations are 2, 3, 3, 5 and 12. Which measure of central tendency best represents a typical observation, and what is its value?
choices: Median of 7, the midpoint of the range
Median of 3, because it is not distorted by the outlier
Mean of 5, because outliers do not affect it
Mean of 5, because it uses all observations
questions.exp: The mean is (2 + 3 + 3 + 5 + 12) / 5 = 5, pulled upward by the 12, while the median (middle value) is 3 and is resistant to outliers. The midpoint of the range, 7, is not the median.

questions.q: Sales for the last three months were 100 (oldest), 120 and 140 (most recent) units. Using a weighted moving average with weights of 3 for the most recent month, 2 for the middle month and 1 for the oldest month, what is next month's forecast?
questions.exp: Forecast = (3 x 140 + 2 x 120 + 1 x 100) / 6 = 760 / 6 = 126.67 units. The 113.33 answer applies the heaviest weight to the oldest month, and 120 is the unweighted average.

questions.q: Last month's forecast was 100 units, and actual demand was 120 units. Using exponential smoothing with a smoothing constant (alpha) of 0.3, what is this month's forecast?
questions.exp: New forecast = prior forecast + alpha x (actual - prior forecast) = 100 + 0.3 x (120 - 100) = 106 units. The 114 answer applies alpha to the prior forecast instead of to the actual demand.

questions.q: A predictive model with 40 explanatory variables fits the historical training data almost perfectly but performs poorly when applied to new data. What is the most likely issue, and how is it usually detected?
choices: Underfitting, detected by adding more variables
Multicollinearity, detected by a high R-squared
Overfitting, detected by testing the model on holdout data
Data latency, detected by refreshing the data more often
questions.exp: An overfit model captures noise in the training data rather than the underlying pattern, so it fails on new data; validation on a holdout or test set reveals this. Adding more variables would make overfitting worse, not better.

questions.q: A marketing team uses an algorithm to group customers into segments based on purchasing behavior, without any predefined segment labels. What type of technique is this?
questions.exp: Clustering is an unsupervised technique that finds natural groupings in unlabeled data. Classification is supervised because it requires training data with known labels.

questions.q: On January 1, Harlan Corp. issued a $1,000,000, 6% fixed-rate note and simultaneously entered into an interest rate swap (receive 6% fixed, pay SOFR) with matching terms, designated as a fair value hedge of the benchmark interest rate risk of the note. At December 31, benchmark rates had fallen and the swap had a fair value of $25,000 (asset); the fair value of the note attributable to the benchmark rate increased by $25,000. What net amount related to these fair value changes is recognized in Harlan's earnings for the year?
questions.exp: In a fair value hedge (ASC 815-25), the $25,000 swap gain and the $25,000 loss from the basis adjustment to the hedged note are both recognized in earnings, so they offset to $0. Recognizing only the swap gain ignores the required adjustment to the carrying amount of the hedged item.

questions.q: Ridley Co. designated a futures contract as a cash flow hedge of a highly probable forecasted inventory purchase. At year-end, the futures contract had a $40,000 gain. Under the prior rules, $3,000 of that gain would have been considered ineffective. Under current ASC 815 guidance, how much of the gain is reported in other comprehensive income at year-end, assuming the hedge remains highly effective?
questions.exp: After ASU 2017-12, the entire change in fair value of a hedging instrument included in the effectiveness assessment of a highly effective cash flow hedge is recorded in OCI, so all $40,000 is deferred; ineffectiveness is no longer separately measured. The $37,000 answer applies the superseded rule that sent the ineffective portion to earnings.

questions.q: On November 1, Benton Inc. entered into a 90-day forward contract to purchase 100,000 euros at a forward rate of $1.10. The contract was not designated as a hedge. On December 31, the forward rate for a contract maturing on the original settlement date was $1.14. Ignoring discounting, how should Benton report the forward contract in its December 31 financial statements?
choices: A $4,000 gain in other comprehensive income
No amount, because the contract is executory
questions.exp: An undesignated derivative is measured at fair value with changes in earnings: 100,000 x ($1.14 - $1.10) = $4,000 gain, since the right to buy euros at $1.10 is worth more when the forward rate rises. OCI treatment applies only to qualifying cash flow or net investment hedges.

questions.q: Delmar Co. purchased a call option on 1,000 shares of Zeta stock with a strike price of $50 for a premium of $3,000 when Zeta was trading at $50. At year-end, Zeta traded at $56 and the option had a fair value of $8,500. The option is not designated as a hedge. What gain should Delmar recognize in earnings for the year?
questions.exp: The option is carried at fair value: $8,500 - $3,000 premium paid = $5,500 gain in earnings. The $6,000 figure is only the intrinsic value change and ignores that the $3,000 time value at purchase declined to $2,500.

questions.q: Fenwick Corp. holds silver inventory with a cost of $200,000 and designated short silver futures as a fair value hedge of the inventory's price risk. During the period, the fair value of the inventory declined by $15,000 and the futures contracts gained $14,000. What is the net effect on Fenwick's earnings for the period?
questions.exp: In a fair value hedge, the hedged inventory is adjusted for the $15,000 decline (loss in earnings) and the futures gain of $14,000 is also in earnings, netting to a $1,000 decrease. Ignoring the inventory basis adjustment would show only the $14,000 gain.

questions.q: Gale Co. had a $40,000 gain in accumulated other comprehensive income from a cash flow hedge of a forecasted inventory purchase. The inventory was purchased in March, and 60% of it was sold by year-end. How much of the deferred gain should be reclassified from AOCI to earnings during the year?
questions.exp: Amounts in AOCI are reclassified when the hedged forecasted transaction affects earnings; for inventory that is when it is sold through cost of goods sold: $40,000 x 60% = $24,000. Reclassifying all $40,000 at purchase date is the common trap—the purchase itself does not affect earnings.

questions.q: Hollis Inc. has $5,000,000 of variable-rate debt bearing interest at SOFR + 1%. It entered into a swap to pay 4% fixed and receive SOFR on $5,000,000, designated as a cash flow hedge. SOFR averaged 3.2% for the year. What total interest expense, including the swap net settlement, should Hollis report?
questions.exp: Debt interest is $5,000,000 x 4.2% = $210,000; the swap requires paying 4% and receiving 3.2%, a net payment of $5,000,000 x 0.8% = $40,000, for total interest of $250,000 (an effective 5% fixed rate). Stopping at $210,000 ignores the swap settlement that converts the debt to fixed.

questions.q: Irving Co. has a $2,000,000, 6% fixed-rate note. It entered into a swap to receive 5% fixed and pay SOFR on a $2,000,000 notional, designated as a fair value hedge. SOFR for the year was 3.5%. Ignoring any fair value changes, what is Irving's net interest expense for the year?
questions.exp: Note interest is $120,000; the swap receives $100,000 (5%) and pays $70,000 (3.5%), a net receipt of $30,000, so net interest is $120,000 - $30,000 = $90,000 (effectively SOFR + 1%). Answering $70,000 counts only the SOFR leg and ignores the 1% spread between the note coupon and the swap's fixed leg.

questions.q: Jessup Corp. firmly committed to buy equipment for 500,000 euros with delivery in three months and entered into a forward contract to buy 500,000 euros at $1.12, designated as a fair value hedge of the firm commitment (effectiveness based on forward rates). On the delivery date, the spot rate was $1.15. At what amount should Jessup record the equipment?
questions.exp: The forward gain of 500,000 x ($1.15 - $1.12) = $15,000 is offset by a $15,000 firm commitment liability, which is closed against the equipment: $575,000 cash price - $15,000 = $560,000, locking in the forward rate. Recording $575,000 ignores the firm commitment basis adjustment required in a fair value hedge.

questions.q: Kimball Co. issued a five-year note whose principal repayment at maturity equals $1,000,000 adjusted by the percentage change in the S&P 500 index over the note's term. Which treatment does ASC 815 require for this feature?
choices: Bifurcate the equity-index feature and account for it as a derivative because it is not clearly and closely related to the debt host
Record the index feature in additional paid-in capital as an equity component
Account for the entire note at amortized cost because the index is a widely published market measure
Bifurcate only if the note is convertible into Kimball's own shares
questions.exp: An equity-indexed principal payment has economic characteristics unrelated to a debt host, so the embedded derivative is not clearly and closely related and must be separated and measured at fair value (ASC 815-15), unless the fair value option is elected for the whole instrument. Being a published index does not make it closely related to interest rates or credit.

questions.q: Lyman Inc. uses the dollar-offset method to assess hedge effectiveness. For the quarter, the change in fair value of the hedged item attributable to the hedged risk was a $100,000 decrease, and the hedging derivative increased $88,000. What is the offset ratio and conclusion?
choices: 88%; not highly effective because the ratio is below 90%
questions.exp: The offset ratio is $88,000 / $100,000 = 88%, which falls within the 80%-125% range generally accepted as highly effective. The 90% threshold is not part of the guidance, and 112% inverts the ratio but would still be within range.

questions.q: Marlow Corp. (USD functional currency) has a net investment of 10 million euros in a German subsidiary and designated 10 million euros of borrowings as a hedge of that net investment. During the year the euro strengthened from $1.10 to $1.15. How is the remeasurement of the euro debt reported?
choices: $500,000 loss in other comprehensive income as part of the cumulative translation adjustment
questions.exp: The euro debt increases by 10,000,000 x $0.05 = $500,000; as an effective net investment hedge, the loss goes to the CTA in OCI, offsetting the translation gain on the net investment (ASC 815-35). Reporting it in net income ignores the designated hedge relationship.

questions.q: Norris Co. entered into a 6-month forward contract to sell 1,000,000 Swiss francs at $1.08. At year-end, three months remain and the forward rate for that settlement date is $1.05. The appropriate discount rate is 8% per year (simple interest). What is the fair value of the forward contract at year-end?
questions.exp: The undiscounted gain is 1,000,000 x ($1.08 - $1.05) = $30,000, receivable in 3 months; discounting gives $30,000 / (1 + 0.08 x 3/12) = $30,000 / 1.02 = $29,412. The $27,778 answer discounts for a full year instead of three months.

questions.q: Oakes Co. purchased an at-the-money currency option for a $12,000 premium (all time value) and designated it as a cash flow hedge of a forecasted purchase 12 months away. It excluded time value from the effectiveness assessment and elected to recognize the excluded component in earnings using a systematic and rational amortization approach. The option was purchased September 1. How much of the excluded component is recognized in earnings for the year ended December 31?
questions.exp: Under ASU 2017-12, the initial value of an excluded component may be amortized into earnings over the hedge term: $12,000 x 4/12 = $4,000 for September through December. Recognizing $0 would defer the entire time value in OCI, which the amortization election does not allow.

questions.q: Pruitt Farms bought five corn futures contracts of 5,000 bushels each at $4.50 per bushel and posted initial margin of $2,000 per contract. The contracts were not designated as hedges. At year-end, the futures price was $4.30. What should Pruitt report in earnings?
choices: $0, because only the margin deposit has been paid
questions.exp: The futures loss is 25,000 bushels x ($4.50 - $4.30) = $5,000, recognized in earnings because the contracts are undesignated derivatives. The margin deposit is a separate asset, and $1,000 uses only one contract's bushels.

questions.q: Quinlan Corp. has a $30,000 gain in AOCI from a cash flow hedge of a forecasted sale. Quinlan discontinued hedge accounting because the forecasted sale is no longer probable, though it is still reasonably possible that it will occur within an additional two months. How much of the AOCI gain should be reclassified to earnings immediately?
choices: $0; the gain remains in AOCI until the forecasted transaction affects earnings or becomes probable of not occurring
$15,000 to earnings, with the remainder in AOCI
questions.exp: Under ASC 815-30-40, amounts stay in AOCI after discontinuance unless it is probable that the forecasted transaction will not occur within the original period or the additional two-month window. Immediate reclassification is the trap; it is required only when occurrence becomes probable of not happening.

questions.q: Ross Co. holds an available-for-sale fixed-rate debt security and designated a swap as a fair value hedge of its benchmark interest rate risk. During the year, the security's fair value fell $50,000, of which $42,000 was attributable to the benchmark rate and $8,000 to other non-credit factors. The swap gained $41,000. What is the effect on Ross's net income?
questions.exp: In a fair value hedge of an AFS security, the change attributable to the hedged risk ($42,000 loss) moves from OCI to earnings and offsets the $41,000 swap gain, a $1,000 decrease; the $8,000 unhedged change stays in OCI. The $9,000 answer puts the entire security decline in earnings.

questions.q: Sutton Inc. wrote a put option on 1,000 shares of a listed stock and received a $5,000 premium. At year-end, the fair value of the written option was $9,000. The option is not a hedge. What should Sutton recognize in earnings for the year?
questions.exp: The written option is a liability initially recorded at the $5,000 premium and remeasured to $9,000, producing a $4,000 loss. Recognizing the premium as a $5,000 gain ignores that it is a liability carried at fair value.

questions.q: Taft Co. designated a receive-fixed, pay-variable swap as a fair value hedge of its fixed-rate debt. Under current ASC 815 presentation requirements, where is the change in the swap's fair value reported in the income statement?
choices: Other income, separate from the hedged item
Interest expense, the same line as the earnings effect of the hedged debt
A separate hedging gains and losses line below operating income
questions.exp: ASU 2017-12 requires the change in fair value of a fair value hedging instrument to be presented in the same income statement line as the earnings effect of the hedged item—here, interest expense. OCI is used for cash flow and net investment hedges, not fair value hedges.

questions.q: Underwood Corp. wants to apply the shortcut method to a receive-fixed, pay-SOFR swap hedging its fixed-rate debt. Which fact would preclude use of the shortcut method?
choices: The variable leg of the swap is indexed to SOFR
The swap's notional amount equals the debt's principal
The swap had a fair value of $40,000 at inception because its fixed rate was off-market
The swap's expiration date matches the debt's maturity
questions.exp: The shortcut method requires the swap's fair value at inception to be zero (ASC 815-20-25-104); an off-market swap with a $40,000 initial value fails that condition. Matching notional, matching maturity, and a benchmark variable rate such as SOFR are all consistent with the shortcut method.

questions.q: In October, Vance Airlines bought futures for 50,000 gallons of jet fuel at $2.40 per gallon, designated as a cash flow hedge of a March fuel purchase. At December 31, the futures price was $2.60. In March, Vance bought the fuel at the spot price of $2.75 and closed the futures at $2.75. When the fuel is consumed, what total fuel expense is recognized?
questions.exp: The total futures gain is 50,000 x ($2.75 - $2.40) = $17,500, deferred in AOCI and reclassified when the fuel is consumed: $137,500 - $17,500 = $120,000 (the locked-in $2.40 price). The $127,500 answer offsets only the $10,000 gain recorded through December 31.

questions.q: Walsh Co. has an interest rate swap with a $10,000,000 notional amount under which it pays 3.5% fixed and receives SOFR. For the current annual period, SOFR was reset at 4.1%. What is the net settlement for the period?
questions.exp: Walsh receives 4.1% and pays 3.5%, so it receives the net 0.6% x $10,000,000 = $60,000; swaps settle net rather than gross. Paying $60,000 reverses the direction of the legs.

questions.q: Yardley Inc. designated a forward contract to sell 100,000,000 yen at $0.0070 as a cash flow hedge of a forecasted yen-denominated sale. The sale occurred when the spot rate was $0.0066, and the forward was settled at that date. What total revenue does Yardley report for the sale, including amounts reclassified from AOCI?
questions.exp: Revenue at spot is 100,000,000 x $0.0066 = $660,000; the forward gain of 100,000,000 x $0.0004 = $40,000 is reclassified from AOCI into revenue when the sale affects earnings, for $700,000 total—the hedged rate. The $620,000 answer subtracts the gain instead of adding it.

questions.q: Zeller Corp., a public business entity, entered into an interest rate swap on January 1 to hedge fixed-rate debt but did not prepare formal hedge documentation until March 31. Between January 1 and March 31, the swap's fair value increased $18,000 and the fair value of the debt attributable to the benchmark rate increased $18,000. What is the effect on Zeller's first-quarter earnings?
questions.exp: Hedge accounting applies only from the date formal documentation is in place, so for January through March the swap is an undesignated derivative and its $18,000 gain goes to earnings with no offsetting basis adjustment on the debt. Answering $0 assumes hedge accounting was available retroactively.

questions.q: Which of the following contracts entered into by Abbott Manufacturing is accounted for as a derivative under ASC 815?
choices: A five-year interest rate swap with a $5,000,000 notional amount and no initial payment
Stock options granted to employees as compensation
A forward contract to buy shares of a privately held company requiring gross physical delivery, with no market mechanism to settle net
A contract to buy steel for use in production with physical delivery in quantities expected to be used, documented under the normal purchases exception
questions.exp: The swap has an underlying and notional amount, no initial net investment, and settles net, meeting the ASC 815-10-15-83 definition. The steel contract qualifies for the normal purchases scope exception, the private-share forward fails net settlement, and employee share-based awards are in ASC 718's scope.

questions.q: Baxter Co. entered into a pay-fixed, receive-SOFR swap as a highly effective cash flow hedge of its variable-rate debt. Rates rose during the year, and at December 31 the swap had a fair value of $75,000 (asset). Baxter's tax rate is 25%. Assuming no reclassifications, what amount should be in AOCI related to the swap at December 31, net of tax?
questions.exp: The $75,000 swap gain is deferred in OCI for an effective cash flow hedge and presented net of deferred tax: $75,000 x (1 - 25%) = $56,250. The $75,000 answer ignores the related deferred tax effect.

questions.q: Carver Corp. has variable-rate debt and has designated a pay-fixed, receive-variable swap as a cash flow hedge. If market interest rates decline significantly, how is the swap affected?
choices: The swap becomes a liability, with the loss deferred in other comprehensive income
The swap's fair value does not change because the debt rate also declines
The swap becomes a liability, with the loss recognized as an adjustment to the debt's carrying amount
The swap becomes an asset, with the gain recognized in earnings
questions.exp: When rates fall, paying fixed and receiving a lower variable rate is unfavorable, so the swap becomes a liability; in an effective cash flow hedge the loss goes to OCI and is reclassified as interest is paid. Adjusting the debt's carrying amount is a fair value hedge treatment.

questions.q: Dunn Oil entered into a monthly commodity swap on 10,000 barrels under which it pays a fixed $80 per barrel and receives the average index price. For the current month, the average index price was $86 per barrel. What is the net settlement for the month?
questions.exp: Dunn receives $86 and pays $80 per barrel, a net receipt of 10,000 x $6 = $60,000; the swap settles net, not gross. Paying $60,000 reverses the direction of the legs.

questions.q: Which of the following hedging relationships is prohibited from receiving hedge accounting under ASC 815?
choices: A cash flow hedge of variable interest receipts on an available-for-sale debt security
A fair value hedge of interest rate risk on fixed-rate debt issued by the entity
A fair value hedge of the interest rate risk of a held-to-maturity debt security
A net investment hedge using foreign-currency-denominated debt
questions.exp: ASC 815-20-25-43 prohibits designating interest rate risk of a held-to-maturity security as the hedged risk, since the entity has asserted it will hold the security to maturity regardless of rate changes (hedging the prepayment option component is the narrow exception). The other relationships are all eligible.

questions.q: On December 1, Ellery Co. sold goods for 200,000 British pounds on 60-day credit when the spot rate was $1.25 and simultaneously entered into a 60-day forward contract to sell 200,000 pounds at $1.24 (not designated as a hedge). At December 31, the spot rate was $1.22 and the forward rate for the remaining 30 days was $1.215. Ignoring discounting, what is the net effect on December earnings?
questions.exp: The receivable loses 200,000 x ($1.25 - $1.22) = $6,000 (spot rate remeasurement), and the forward gains 200,000 x ($1.24 - $1.215) = $5,000, for a net $1,000 loss. Reporting only the $6,000 receivable loss ignores the forward that acts as a natural hedge through earnings.

questions.q: Before issuing 10-year fixed-rate bonds, Finch Corp. entered into a treasury lock designated as a cash flow hedge of the forecasted interest payments. Rates rose before issuance, and Finch settled the lock for a $120,000 gain, which was deferred in AOCI. Assuming the gain is reclassified in equal annual amounts as a yield adjustment, how does the gain affect the first full year after issuance?
choices: Interest expense is reduced by $120,000 at issuance
Other income of $120,000 is recognized at settlement
questions.exp: The deferred gain is reclassified from AOCI as the hedged interest payments affect earnings, reducing interest expense by about $120,000 / 10 = $12,000 per year. Recognizing the full gain at settlement ignores that the hedged transactions are the future interest payments.

questions.q: Gilman Inc. issued a hybrid debt instrument for $1,000,000 cash. Gilman determined that an embedded derivative must be bifurcated and that its fair value at issuance is $70,000. At what amount should the host debt contract be initially recorded?
questions.exp: The embedded derivative is recorded at fair value, and the host contract receives the residual: $1,000,000 - $70,000 = $930,000, with the difference accreted as additional interest. Adding the derivative value to proceeds reverses the with-and-without allocation.

questions.q: Harper Co. has an interest rate swap with two annual settlements remaining on a $1,000,000 notional, under which it receives 5% fixed and pays a variable rate. The market expects the variable rate to be 4% for both remaining years, and the appropriate discount rate is 4%. What is the swap's fair value to Harper?
questions.exp: Expected net receipts are $1,000,000 x 1% = $10,000 per year; PV = $10,000/1.04 + $10,000/1.04^2 = $9,615 + $9,246 = $18,861. The $20,000 answer ignores discounting, and $19,231 discounts both payments for only one period.

questions.q: Ingram Co. holds equity securities measured at fair value through net income. It purchased put options on the same securities as an economic hedge. During the year the securities declined $30,000 and the puts gained $26,000. What is the net effect on Ingram's net income?
choices: $30,000 decrease, with the $26,000 gain reported in OCI
questions.exp: Both the equity securities (ASC 321) and the undesignated puts are measured at fair value through net income, so the net effect is -$30,000 + $26,000 = $4,000 decrease; hedge accounting is unnecessary and not permitted for items already remeasured through earnings. Putting the put gain in OCI wrongly applies cash flow hedge treatment.

questions.q: Jarvis Corp. deferred a $50,000 gain in AOCI from a cash flow hedge of the forecasted purchase of equipment. The equipment was acquired on January 1 and is depreciated straight-line over 10 years with no salvage value. How much of the deferred gain is reclassified into earnings in the first year?
questions.exp: The hedged forecasted purchase affects earnings through depreciation, so the gain is reclassified as an offset to depreciation over the asset's life: $50,000 / 10 = $5,000. Reclassifying the entire $50,000 at purchase ignores that buying equipment does not affect earnings.

questions.q: Kessler Co. assesses hedge effectiveness using regression analysis. For a proposed hedge, the regression of changes in the derivative's value on changes in the hedged item's value produced a slope of -0.92 and an R-squared of 0.76. What is the appropriate conclusion?
choices: Not highly effective, because the slope is negative
Highly effective, because the slope is within the -0.80 to -1.25 range
